sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content, representativeness and data quality of the reference data set (RDS) of the LGD model for Dutch residential mortgages (LGD-MORT-NL, model identifier MDL-02, model version 3.1). The RDS serves the estimation and calibration of the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default used for the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach, and it is also the data basis for the annual review of estimates. The scope of application covers all retail exposures secured by residential property in the Netherlands booked in the Bank's mortgage administration system, including loans with a Nationale Hypotheek Garantie (NHG) and loans secured by second-ranking mortgage rights. The document follows the RDS template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A (v3.0); template sections that do not apply are retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification, and added sections are placed after the last template section of the relevant chapter. It replaces the data chapter of the legacy MDD v2.3 (2023), in line with the migration rule of MRM-STD-021 section 9.1. The RDS documentation is one of the four mandatory documents of MDL-02: the RDS documentation (this document), the MDD LGD Mortgages (EVD-02-MDD v1.0), the implementation specification IS-LGDM-3.1 with the implementation and testing report EVD-02-IMPL, and the monitoring plan in chapter 10 of the MDD. Figures in this document are produced from the frozen RDS LGDMORT_RDS_v2025.1, which is also referenced in chapter 3 of the MDD, so that the RDS documentation, the MDD and the implementation specification refer to the same data version. Documents referred to are identified with document identifier and version and are held in the controlled repository accessible to Model Validation, so that the documentation does not rely on undocumented knowledge. The applicable requirement set was derived from the requirement library at the start of the 2025 recalibration (requirement set RS-2025-022) and was used to plan the evidence in this document. In the 1LoD self-assessment, every evidence reference points to a section number of this approved version.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains all default events of in-scope facilities with a date of default between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2023 (16 years), with recovery cash flows, costs and status information observed up to the cut-off date of 31 December 2024. The unit of observation is the mortgage loan (facility), comprising all loan parts secured by the same mortgage deed; recovery cash flows are recorded monthly per facility. After the treatments described in chapter 4 the RDS holds 31,206 default events on 31,206 facilities of 28,470 unique obligors, and 1,184,650 facility-months of cash-flow records. Of the 31,206 default events, 29,418 (94.3%) relate to closed recovery processes and 1,788 (5.7%) to incomplete recovery processes, mainly defaults of 2021 to 2023. The observation period exceeds the minimum of five years required by CRR Article 181(2) for retail LGD and includes all relevant internal loss data available in the Bank's systems; it consists of consecutive years up to and including the most recent complete default year. All defaults observed in the observation period within the range of application are included, except the technical past due situations and duplicate records described in section 4.2 and the 94 legacy defaults without cash-flow history.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2008 because the workout database of Financial Restructuring & Recovery (FR&R) holds complete facility-level recovery cash flows from that date; recovery data before 2008 were kept at aggregated portfolio level only and cannot be allocated to facilities. The window covers the global financial crisis of 2008–2009, the Dutch housing market correction of 2008–2013 (nominal house prices fell by 21% peak to trough), the peak in mortgage arrears in 2013–2014, the benign years 2016–2021 and the interest rate increases of 2022–2023. It therefore contains a representative mix of good and bad years and includes the downturn period identified in chapter 5 of the MDD, so that the long-run average LGD is representative of long-run experience. The economic conditions in the window are considered relevant for current and foreseeable conditions: the legal framework for forced sales (Article 3:268 of the Dutch Civil Code), the NHG scheme and the Bank's recovery process have remained in place throughout, while the effects of changes are analysed in section 5.1.3. With 31,206 defaults and 6,382 closed liquidation cases the number of observations is sufficient for robust estimation of the cure and liquidation components in both calibration segments, the smallest pool containing 611 defaults. Defaults under the definition of default implemented on 1 December 2020 are included from that date; in each annual review the window is extended with the most recent default year so that the share of defaults under the current definition increases, and the related MoC is reassessed.

sections.heading: Default cohorts and status of recovery processes
sections.text: Annex B, table B.1 shows per default year the number of defaults, the share of closed recovery processes and the average realised LGD over all defaults of that year that are closed or have reached the maximum recovery period of 60 months. Default counts rise from 1,212 in 2008 to a peak of 3,634 in 2013, fall to 1,009 in 2021 and increase again to 1,529 in 2023. A recovery process is treated as closed when the facility has returned to non-defaulted status, has been fully repaid, has been written off after sale of the collateral and final settlement of the residual debt, or when the maximum recovery period of 60 months after default has been exceeded; closure is recorded without delay in the monthly RDS update. The maximum recovery period of 60 months is supported by the recovery pattern of closed processes: 98.6% of the discounted recoveries of closed liquidation cases are received within 60 months of default, and the marginal recovery after month 60 is below 0.2% of the outstanding amount at default. For the 1,788 incomplete recovery processes, the cash flows observed up to the cut-off date are retained in the RDS and future recoveries are estimated in the MDD on the basis of the observed recovery patterns of closed processes of comparable time in default, applying a conservative treatment where the pattern is uncertain. Annual default counts are reported at each reference date, so that as many points in time are available for the impact analysis as the data allow and no default years are merged.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: Not applicable in the sense of the template condition: the target is the realised LGD of the regulatory default event defined in section 3.3, and no fixed 12-month outcome horizon is used. Realised LGD is measured over the complete recovery process, from the date of default until closure or the maximum recovery period of 60 months, as specified in section 4.4. For the cure component the target is the binary outcome whether the facility returns to non-defaulted status within the recovery process; for the liquidation component the target is the loss given liquidation of facilities whose recovery process ended with the sale of the collateral or another non-cure closure. Both component targets are derived from the same default events, so that the same definition of default is applied to the historical observations used in the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and to the observations used by the mortgage PD model MDL-01 for the overlapping period 2012–2023. For defaulted exposures, additional targets are defined per reference date in default (section 4.4.4).

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For default events between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2015 the default flag is approximated, because the components of the current definition (daily days-past-due counters with materiality thresholds, UTP flags and probation status) have been captured in the source systems only since 1 January 2016 (CR-STD-110 section 9.3). For this period a default is set when the monthly arrears amount exceeds three monthly instalments and EUR 100 at a month-end, or when the arrears management system records a forced-sale procedure, a distressed restructuring or a bankruptcy or debt-rescheduling (WSNP) registration. On the 2016–2019 overlap period, the approximation identifies 96.8% of the defaults under the reconstructed current definition and generates 2.1% additional defaults; the resulting average realised LGD differs by -0.2 percentage points, the approximation producing slightly more cures. Probation periods cannot be reconstructed for 2008–2015; for these years a return to non-default is recognised only after three consecutive month-ends without arrears above the threshold, which is identified as data deficiency DD-LGDM-01 and covered by MoC component A1. From 1 January 2016 to 30 November 2020 the default flag is reconstructed from daily data with the current definition, and from 1 December 2020 the production default flag under CR-STD-110 v2.0 is used; each of the three definitions is analysed separately in Annex B, table B.4. The regulatory materiality threshold of EUR 100 and 1% has been applied in production since 1 December 2020, the date of application set by De Nederlandsche Bank, and the RDS field DEF_FLAG_SOURCE identifies for every default event whether the approximated, reconstructed or production flag applies.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: A default occurs when the obligor is more than 90 consecutive days past due on a material credit obligation or when the obligor is considered unlikely to pay, in accordance with CRR Article 178 and CR-STD-110. Days past due are counted from the first day on which both the absolute component of EUR 100 and the relative component of 1% of the materiality threshold for retail exposures are exceeded, and counting restarts at zero when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component is that sum divided by the total on-balance-sheet exposure of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, excluding equity exposures. The relative threshold of 1% applied is the level set by De Nederlandsche Bank for all institutions in its jurisdiction; no lower internal threshold is used as a UTP indication. An obligor is defaulted under the past due criterion when both components are exceeded for 90 consecutive days, and the default flag is activated at the onset of the 91st consecutive day; no months-in-arrears proxy is used for the period covered by the production flag. Days past due are computed daily in the arrears management system (AMS), and the date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met; it is recorded for every default event in the field DEF_DATE. Once the past due criterion is met the obligor is classified as defaulted without further expert judgement, unless a technical past due situation is confirmed. The thresholds are expressed in euro and all exposures in scope are denominated in euro, so that the currency provisions of Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 do not apply.

sections.heading: Level of application, joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: The definition of default is applied at obligor level, in line with the Bank's risk management practice for retail mortgages, where arrears management, forbearance and recovery decisions are taken per household; the level of application has not changed over the observation period. As the facility-level option for retail exposures is not used, the facility-level materiality threshold and the facility-level calculation of Article 1(3) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 do not apply. When an obligor defaults, all credit obligations of the obligor with the Bank, including consumer loans and current account overdrafts, are flagged as defaulted in all relevant systems. Most mortgages are joint credit obligations of two partners; a joint obligation is treated as a separate obligor in the materiality threshold calculation, and the default of the joint obligation is propagated to the individual exposures of both partners unless Credit Risk Management documents that the para 97 exceptions of EBA/GL/2016/07 apply. Contagion between connected obligors is assessed case by case by FR&R for obligors who also hold business loans; the outcome is recorded in the default register. The same definition of default is applied by all Group entities holding Dutch residential mortgages, so that the RDS does not combine different default definitions.

sections.heading: Counting of days past due
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on the due date is recognised as past due, including arrears on loan parts with deferred interest and on linked bank savings accounts. Where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the basis of the modified schedule, and every modification granted because of financial difficulties is assessed as a potential distressed restructuring (section 3.4). Instalments suspended under the statutory or contractual payment holidays of 2020 are not counted as past due; the reasons for the suspensions were analysed and 214 obligors were assessed as unlikely to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed amounts only where the dispute is before a court or before the Dutch Financial Services Complaints Institute (Kifid). Technical past due is recognised only for data or system errors of the Bank, failures of the payment system and payment allocation time lags; each case is documented, corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management, and wrong credit decisions are never treated as technical past due. The Bank's policy on the re-ageing of facilities, extensions and deferrals, renewals and the netting of accounts is documented in the arrears management procedure AMS-PRC-04 v3.2, which prohibits re-ageing without a formal forbearance decision. Technical past due events identified in the RDS (1,014 events) are removed from the set of defaulted exposures used for estimation (section 4.2).

sections.heading: Return to non-defaulted status, probation and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-defaulted status only when no default trigger continues to apply, after a probation period of at least three months in which no past due or UTP condition is met, and after an assessment by FR&R that the improvement in credit quality is factual and permanent, including a review of payment behaviour and income. For obligors defaulted because of a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring, the default classification and the end of any grace period. During this period the obligor must make regular payments totalling at least the amount previously past due or written off, have no amount past due and show no UTP indication or doubt about full repayment, including for schedules with a large final instalment. The probation start date and probation status are recorded for every default event in the fields PROB_START and PROB_STATUS. A new triggering of a default event after return to non-defaulted status is treated as a new default, subject to the multiple default treatment in section 3.3.4. Where a facility defaults again within 12 months of returning to non-defaulted status, both events are treated as a single default starting on the first date of default; the 12-month period is longer than the nine months of EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 101 and is justified by the re-default analysis in Annex B, table B.6, which shows that 71% of re-defaults of mortgages occur within 12 months after cure. The RDS links default events of the same facility through the field DEF_CHAIN_ID; in the observation period 2,386 default events were merged into a preceding default, and the merged events are listed in Annex B, table B.6. For merged defaults the outstanding amount at the first default date is used and all cash flows of both events are included in the economic loss; the artificial cure cash flow of the first event is removed. The treatment is identical in the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and it is applied consistently in the annual review datasets.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: The UTP triggers of CR-STD-110 are applied as follows: non-accrued status, specific credit risk adjustments including IFRS 9 Stage 3 classification, sale of a credit obligation at a credit-related economic loss above 5%, distressed restructuring with a diminished financial obligation above 1%, bankruptcy or debt-rescheduling (WSNP) of the obligor and the start of a forced sale of the collateral lead to default automatically. Mortgages whose interest is no longer recognised in the income statement because of a decline in credit quality are flagged as non-accrued and treated as defaulted. Specific credit risk adjustments are UTP indications when they result from a significant decline in credit quality, whereas collective allowances in Stages 1 and 2 are not; all exposures in IFRS 9 Stage 3 are defaulted, as the Bank applies the same definition for Stage 3 and regulatory default. For each forbearance measure the diminished financial obligation is calculated as (NPV0 - NPV1)/NPV0, discounting the expected cash flows before and after the measure at the original effective interest rate, and exposures with a value above 1% are defaulted. Forborne exposures below the threshold are assessed for other indications such as a large final payment, irregular or back-loaded schedules, grace periods above 12 months and repeated forbearance; all forborne non-performing exposures are defaulted. Sales of defaulted mortgage portfolios are analysed for their credit-related loss L = (E - P)/E, with a threshold of 5%; the 146 facilities sold in the 2019 non-performing loan transaction were already defaulted before the sale.

sections.heading: Additional indications and case-by-case assessment
sections.text: Additional UTP indicators for mortgages are defined in the arrears management procedure: unemployment or loss of income of the main earner registered in AMS, divorce with an unresolved residual debt, a negative BKR registration at another lender, fraud, and a request for a second forbearance measure within 24 months. These indicators lead to a case-by-case assessment by FR&R completed within 30 days of detection, and the outcome and rationale of every assessment are recorded in the default register. UTP identification uses external information, including the BKR credit register (daily), WSNP and bankruptcy publications in the Central Insolvency Register (daily) and notifications by NHG, as well as the macroeconomic early-warning dashboard of Credit Risk Management. For each indication the identification method, the internal and external information sources and the monitoring frequency are defined in Annex A, table A.3, which maps each trigger to its source-system fields. Because the UTP flag after case-by-case assessment depends on human judgement, FR&R applies the labelling guideline UTP-GL-02, and Credit Risk Management performs a semi-annual consistency review of assessments across the three regional FR&R teams; the 2025 review found no systematic differences (agreement rate 97.4% on a re-assessed sample of 150 cases).

sections.heading: Default identification process and controls
sections.text: Automatic triggers (days past due, forced sale, bankruptcy and WSNP registration, Stage 3 and non-accrual) are identified daily by AMS; manual triggers from watch lists, forbearance lists and specific provisions are updated at least weekly, which ensures timely identification of default. A monthly control verifies that all forborne non-performing exposures are flagged as defaulted, and forborne performing exposures are reviewed quarterly for UTP indications. All exposures of a defaulted obligor are flagged in AMS, the mortgage administration system and the credit risk data warehouse within one business day; recording delays are monitored and did not affect the default dates in the RDS. The default triggers of CRR Article 178 are implemented identically across all systems and legal entities holding Dutch mortgages, and completeness of default identification is controlled by a monthly reconciliation between AMS and the default register. The operationalisation of each trigger, including process, information sources and responsibilities, is documented in the default identification handbook DoD-HB-MORT v2.1. Internal Audit reviewed the robustness, effectiveness and timeliness of the default identification process in audit IA-2025-017 (report of 14 October 2025, rating Adequate), with conclusions reported to the Management Board.

sections.heading: Consistency of the default definition across uses and over time
sections.text: The same definition of default is used for the IRB approach, IFRS 9 Stage 3, non-performing exposure reporting and credit risk management, and it is the basis for arrears monitoring and internal reporting to management. The definition and its scope of application were approved by the Management Board on the recommendation of the Model Risk Committee on 24 November 2020 (CR-STD-110 v2.0). The register of current and past default definitions maintained by Credit Risk Management records for each version the scope, the approving body and date, the implementation date, the description of changes, the change category under Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014 and the supervisory dates. The RDS default flag is constructed in accordance with CR-STD-110, including materiality thresholds, UTP triggers, probation periods and the multiple default treatment, and the definition used internally is consistent with CRR Article 178. For 2021–2023 the RDS default flag was reconciled with the production default flag: 99.7% of default events match on facility and date, and the 94 differences are explained by retroactive corrections of technical past due. The IRB and IFRS 9 default flags are reconciled quarterly between the risk and finance systems; the Q4 2025 reconciliation showed no unexplained differences. The accounting default (Stage 3) and prudential default are labelled distinctly in the Group Data Catalogue (DEF_PRUD and STAGE3_FLAG), and the definitional relationship between them is documented. No legal impediments to intra-group data exchange exist for Dutch mortgages, so that default identification is not affected.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is built from five source systems: the mortgage administration system (HYPO, since 2011; legacy system HYPO-L before), the arrears management system (AMS), the FR&R workout database (RECOV), the collateral valuation database (CVD) and the general ledger (GL) for write-offs and costs. External inputs are the CBS/Kadaster house price index for existing owner-occupied dwellings (PBK) per province, received monthly from CBS, 3-month EURIBOR fixings received daily from the market data service, and NHG claim settlements received monthly from Stichting Waarborgfonds Eigen Woningen (WEW). Extraction reference dates are the month-ends from January 2008 to December 2024; the snapshot extracted on 7 February 2025 is the source for the frozen RDS. Every RDS variable is traced from its source table and field through the intermediate stores of the credit risk data warehouse (CRDW) to the RDS field in Annex A, which documents each transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the build code module and to the extraction frequency and timing. The lineage includes discarded variables used to construct retained variables, such as the loan-part level balances used to derive the facility outstanding amount. For each type of risk data an authoritative source is defined: HYPO for balances and contract data, AMS for arrears and default flags, RECOV for recovery cash flows, CVD for valuations and GL for write-offs and cost allocation. One manual input exists: the mapping of legacy HYPO-L product codes to current product groups, a version-controlled file whose lineage entry identifies the four-eyes control applied.

sections.heading: Data ownership, metadata and change control
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from four data domains of the Group Data Catalogue: Mortgage Lending, Credit Risk, Recovery and Collateral, each with exactly one Data Owner recorded in the catalogue, and the model data is mapped to these domains in Annex A. Roles and responsibilities for data ownership and data quality are defined for the business (Data Owners and Data Stewards) and for IT (application owners of HYPO, AMS, RECOV and CVD). The model owner agreed the data quality expectations for the critical data elements with the four Data Owners in the data quality agreement DQA-LGDM-2025 of 30 January 2025. Metadata for every RDS data element (business and technical definition, type and format, permitted values, unit and currency, source, Data Owner, update frequency and classification) are recorded in the Group Data Catalogue, and metadata changes are versioned so that the definition applicable to any historical data point can be retrieved. The catalogue uses the Group-wide identifiers for customers (CUST_ID), facilities (FAC_ID) and collateral (COLL_ID) and the naming conventions of the integrated data taxonomy. Changes to the definition, source or transformation logic of these elements are approved by the Data Owner and communicated to the model owner in advance through the data change calendar, and the lineage is updated before changed data is used; the 2019 migration of CVD was processed this way. Data governance for the model inputs thus follows the Bank's data governance framework under DATA-POL-001, which implements the ECB expectations on risk data aggregation.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Starting from 34,912 default events of in-scope facilities, 2,386 events were merged into preceding defaults (section 3.3.4), leaving 32,526 events; the following exclusions were then applied, each approved by the model owner. E1 technical past due: 1,014 events (3.1% of events; 0.9% of outstanding amount at default) removed because they are not defaults under CR-STD-110. E2 duplicate records created by the 2011 migration from HYPO-L: 212 events (0.7%), removed after confirming that the retained record holds all cash flows. E3 legacy defaults of the former brand portfolio without facility-level cash flows: 94 events (0.3%; defaults of 2008–2010), excluded because realised LGD cannot be calculated; this is data deficiency DD-LGDM-03. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records or exposure in any segment, and together they reduce the number of events by 4.1% to 31,206. The conclusion of the impact analysis (section 5.3) is that E1 and E2 do not affect the realised LGD distribution and that E3 has an estimated effect of +0.03 percentage points on the long-run average LGD, which is covered by MoC component A4. No other default observed in the observation period within the scope of the model is excluded; the 146 facilities sold in the 2019 transaction are retained with the sale price treated as recovery.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in Annex C, distinguishing values missing at random, values missing for a structural reason and values missing because of a data deficiency. The main cases are the valuation date at origination, missing for 3.1% of facilities originated before 2012 (data deficiency, imputed with the deed registration date from the Kadaster extract), and the property type, missing for 1.4% of facilities (missing at random, imputed with the mode per province). Imputations are performed by code module impute.py with fixed rules, the share of imputed values per variable is reported in Annex C, and re-estimation without the imputed records changes the LGL coefficients by less than 2% of their value. Outliers are identified with documented criteria that are applied identically in development and production: indexed LTV above 250%, time in default above 120 months and cost amounts above 25% of the outstanding amount at default. Indexed LTV is capped at 250% (37 facilities), which changes the LRA LGD by less than 0.01 percentage points; no outliers in the target variable are capped. Missing values and outliers in the target variable and its constituents are not imputed: 58 recovery records with missing booking dates were corrected at source in RECOV, and no records had to be excluded for this reason.

sections.heading: Calculation of realised LGD
sections.text: Realised LGD is calculated for each facility as the ratio of economic loss to the outstanding amount of the credit obligation at default, including principal, accrued interest and fees. Economic loss equals the outstanding amount at default plus material direct and indirect costs discounted to the date of default, minus all recoveries after default discounted to the date of default. Amounts written off or forgiven before or at default, such as waived penalty interest, are added to the outstanding amount at default in both numerator and denominator. Interest and fees capitalised before default are part of the outstanding amount at default; amounts capitalised after default do not increase economic loss, while recoveries on them are included. Additional drawings after default, mainly advances for property tax, insurance premiums and owners' association contributions paid by the Bank to preserve the collateral, are included in economic loss and do not increase the denominator, because the model has no conversion factor for mortgages. Recoveries comprise sale proceeds, NHG claim payments, payments by the obligor, set-off of pledged bank savings deposits and proceeds of residual debt settlements; each cash flow carries its source code. Realised LGDs below zero, which occur for 1.8% of cured facilities because of penalty interest received, are retained unfloored in the RDS and floored at zero in the MDD for the calculation of observed and long-run average LGD.

sections.heading: Direct and indirect costs
sections.text: Direct costs are the external costs attributable to a facility: notary and auction fees, estate agent commissions, valuation fees, legal fees and bailiff costs; they are booked per facility in RECOV and reconciled to the general ledger. Indirect costs are the costs of the FR&R department and of the arrears management teams, allocated per facility using the Bank's cost accounting: EUR 390 per cured case and EUR 2,480 per liquidation case at 2023 price level, derived from the activity-based cost allocation of the Finance department and indexed with the CPI. Material pre-default collection costs of the arrears management teams are included for the months in arrears preceding default, unless already in the outstanding amount or linked to an earlier separate default. For recovery processes closed before 2012, activity data for the indirect cost allocation are not available; the 2012 unit costs deflated with the CPI are applied as an appropriate adjustment, and the residual uncertainty is covered by MoC component A2 (data deficiency DD-LGDM-02). All information needed to calculate direct and indirect costs is stored in the RDS per facility and month, so that the cost components can be traced to their source. Realised LGD therefore includes all material direct and indirect costs and additional drawings after default, as required by CRM-STD-100 section 9.2.

sections.heading: Discounting and cures
sections.text: All recoveries, costs and additional drawings after default are discounted to the date of default with the 3-month EURIBOR fixing on the date of default plus an add-on of 5 percentage points; the EURIBOR fixing is used as observed, including negative values between 2015 and 2022, so that the discount rate ranges from 4.45% to 9.62% over the observation period. For facilities that return to non-defaulted status, economic loss includes an artificial cash flow equal to the outstanding amount at the date of return, discounted to the date of default like the observed cash flows. The average time from default to cure is 9 months and the average realised LGD of cured facilities is 1.2%, reflecting direct and indirect costs and the discounting effect. Liquidations have an average time from default to sale of 21 months and an average realised LGD of 29.6% for closed cases; residual debt after sale is included until settlement, write-off or the maximum recovery period. The Bank does not apply master netting agreements or on-balance sheet netting to mortgages, so that realised LGD is computed on the outstanding amount without netting and no netting cash flows are counted as recoveries; set-off of pledged bank savings deposits after default is recorded as a recovery.

sections.heading: Reference dates in default
sections.text: For the ELBE and the LGD in-default, reference dates in default are defined at 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 36 and 48 months after the date of default and at the date on which a sale agreement for the collateral is signed. The reference dates were set on the basis of the recovery patterns of closed processes: most cures occur within 12 months, sale agreements are typically concluded between 12 and 24 months, and after 48 months the remaining processes consist of residual debt collection. At each reference date, realised LGD is calculated on the outstanding amount at that date, including fees and interest capitalised before it, with all subsequent recoveries, costs and drawings discounted to that date. The RDS contains for every default event and reference date the outstanding amount, the time in default, the recovery status and the indexed collateral value, providing the data used in the MDD for the estimation of ELBE and LGD in-default. The RDS stores, for each defaulted facility, the data used to assign it to an LGD pool in the year before default, the estimated LGD per pool and the realised LGD, as required for retail exposures.

sections.heading: Collateral and NHG data
sections.text: Each facility is secured by a mortgage right on a residential property in the Netherlands; collateral data (type, value, valuation date and method, lien rank and the link to the secured facilities) are recorded in CVD and meet the data quality requirements of MRM-STD-022. Properties are valued at origination by a qualified independent valuer registered with the NRVT, validated by an independent validation institute and independent of the credit decision, at or below market value; values are indexed monthly with the provincial PBK index and fully revalued within three months after default. The valuation policy VAL-POL-RE v4 sets consistent revaluation rules per collateral type and requires more frequent monitoring when the house price index declines by more than 5% in a year. Collateral values used as risk drivers are taken at the reference date twelve months before default and at default, and the indexed value at the earlier date is used where a valuation shortly before default reflects credit deterioration. For the 0.8% of facilities secured by a second-ranking mortgage right, the prior-ranking claim is deducted from the collateral value, reflecting the subordinated position. No collateral consisting of a liability of the obligor is recognised, and all recognised collateral meets CRR Article 181(1)(f); cash flows from ineligible security, such as pledged life insurance policies, are treated as recoveries without collateral while their source is recorded. NHG data comprise the guarantee amount at origination, the annuity-based decline of the guarantee, the own-risk share (10% for loans since 1 January 2014), the claim date, the claim amount, the payment and any rejection with its reason.

sections.heading: Economic indicator data
sections.text: Economic indicators used for the identification of the economic downturn are stored in the RDS environment with their source, delivery date and version: GDP and unemployment from CBS, the PBK house price index from CBS/Kadaster, mortgage arrears registrations from BKR as external default rate, and NHG loss payments published by WEW as external credit loss. These official statistics are considered accurate and reliable; their revisions are tracked, and the 2024 revision of the GDP series did not change the downturn periods. The Bank's mortgage exposures are located in the Netherlands, and the house price index is included once per province group with a material exposure share (North, East, South and West), since provincial price developments differed by up to 6 percentage points in 2013. Sector-specific indicators are not applicable because the exposures are to private households. Commercial data on regional house price indices of a private provider were considered but not acquired, because the official provincial index covers the relevant geographical areas at negligible cost.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness of the RDS for the current portfolio is assessed separately for the data used in risk differentiation (distributions of risk drivers) and for the data underlying risk quantification (loss levels), with the statistical tests and thresholds of CRM-STD-100 section 6.5 and MV-HB-003 section 6. The analysis covers the scope of application, the definition of default, the distribution of risk characteristics, lending standards and recovery policies, as detailed in Annex B. The scope of the RDS equals the current range of application: all Dutch residential mortgages of the Bank including NHG loans, without portfolios acquired from third parties. The definition of default differs only for 2008–2015 (section 3.2), for which the impact is quantified and covered by MoC. The RDS is representative of the current portfolio in risk drivers and in loss levels, subject to the explained shifts reported in sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2. Taken together, the data used to develop the model are representative, of adequate quality and sufficient in length and depth.

sections.heading: Representativeness of risk-driver distributions
sections.text: The distributions of the risk drivers in the RDS, measured twelve months before default, were compared with the performing portfolio at 31 December 2024 using the PSI with ten buckets. Results: indexed LTV PSI 0.19, NHG flag PSI 0.03, interest-only share PSI 0.08, self-employed flag PSI 0.02, property type PSI 0.01 and arrears in the 12 months before the reference date PSI 0.06. The amber PSI for indexed LTV (between 0.10 and 0.25) is explained by the increase in house prices of 98% between 2013 and 2024, which shifted the current portfolio towards low indexed LTV buckets; all buckets of the current portfolio are covered by at least 1,900 defaults in the RDS. As the shift concerns the level of a risk driver included in the model and each LTV bucket is calibrated separately, no bias in the estimates results, and no additional risk driver or subset of observations is required. The PSI for the pool distribution between the RDS and the current portfolio is 0.23 (amber); the pool distribution is monitored quarterly under the monitoring plan.

sections.heading: Lending standards, recovery policies and legal environment
sections.text: Significant changes over the observation period were analysed by comparing RDS data before and after each change: the introduction of the statutory loan-to-value limit (106% in 2013 falling to 100% in 2018), the requirement of full amortisation for tax deductibility from 2013, the 10% own-risk share of NHG from 2014 and the Bank's early-intervention programme for arrears from 2019. Loans originated after 2013 show lower LGL at comparable indexed LTV (−2.4 percentage points), which is conservative for the estimates. The early-intervention programme increased cure rates by 4.1 percentage points for defaults after 2019, which is reflected in the estimates by the inclusion of these defaults, and the related uncertainty is covered by MoC component B1. The recovery process has used private sale under bank supervision as preferred route since 2014, reducing the share of auction sales from 31% of liquidations in 2012 to 9% in 2023; the change is reflected in the property sale discount in the LGL component. Changes in the legal framework were limited: the right of summary execution of Article 3:268 of the Dutch Civil Code remained unchanged and the NHG terms were updated annually without affecting enforceability.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The LGD components are used outside the own funds calculation in the IFRS 9 ECL model for mortgages (MDL-07) and in the risk-adjusted pricing tool of Retail Mortgages; both uses concern the same population as the RDS. For IFRS 9, MDL-07 uses the best estimate LGD components before downturn adjustment and MoC with forward-looking HPI scenarios, so that the RDS is representative for this use; differences between the IRB and internal parameters are documented in chapter 1 of the MDD. The pricing tool uses the final IRB LGD per pool including MoC and floor, so that no separate representativeness analysis is required. The model is not used for mortgages of other Group entities or for buy-to-let mortgages, which are outside the range of application; a use for such portfolios would require a representativeness analysis before extension.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The effect of each exclusion on the distribution of risk drivers and on realised LGD was quantified on the 32,526 events before exclusions. E1 (technical past due) has no effect on risk-driver distributions (PSI 0.01) and would lower the LRA LGD by 0.05 percentage points if retained, because technical past due events cure immediately. E2 (duplicates) has no effect, because the retained records carry all cash flows. E3 (former brand legacy defaults) concerns 94 defaults of 2008–2010 with an average indexed LTV of 91% compared with 84% for retained defaults of the same years; assigning them the realised LGD of retained defaults with similar LTV and NHG status increases the LRA LGD by 0.03 percentage points. The aggregate effect of all exclusions on the long-run average LGD is therefore +0.03 percentage points, reported to Model Validation with the RDS and covered by MoC component A4.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality assessment of the RDS was performed before estimation under MRM-STD-022 and is reported in full in EVD-02-DQ; this section summarises the results. All 41 RDS variables, including the 12 candidate risk drivers and the 18 data elements used to construct the target variable (default flag, default date, outstanding amount at default, recovery cash flows, costs and write-offs), are designated as critical data elements. Data quality was assessed on completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, and additionally on validity, uniqueness and appropriateness, with at least one rule per critical data element for each applicable dimension (318 rules in total). All rules use the default amber and red thresholds of MRM-STD-022 section 4.3 or stricter thresholds; for the default flag and the recovery cash flows the accuracy thresholds are tightened to 0.25% (amber) and 0.5% (red). Of the 318 rules, 309 are green, 9 amber and none red; the amber results concern the completeness of the valuation date at origination and of the indirect cost allocation before 2012 and are recorded as data deficiencies in section 6.2. The assessment concluded that the RDS is fit for the estimation of the performing LGD, ELBE and LGD in-default, and it was signed off by the model developer and the model owner on 21 February 2025 before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and accuracy
sections.text: The outstanding amount at default was reconciled to HYPO and the write-offs to the general ledger: for 2016–2023 the difference is 0.12% of outstanding amounts and 0.21% of write-offs, within the tightened thresholds. Record counts per reference date were reconciled with the monthly default register extracts, and every default event was reconciled to the default register maintained under CR-STD-110, with 99.7% agreement for 2021–2023 and explained differences for earlier years. A sample of 400 recovery files (200 cures and 200 liquidations) was verified against source documentation such as notarial settlement statements and NHG claim letters; seven date discrepancies (1.75%) and no amount discrepancies above EUR 100 were found. The critical data elements of the RDS are reconciled against source and accounting data at least annually as part of the review of estimates, and unexplained differences are recorded as data quality issues. RDS data used for own funds calculation are reconcilable with the accounting data and with the COREP C 08 exposure data of the same reference date.

sections.heading: Data quality controls in the data flow
sections.text: Data quality controls operate from data entry to the RDS: input validations in HYPO and RECOV, automated reconciliations between AMS, HYPO and the general ledger in CRDW, and the 318 RDS rules implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool (Collibra DQ). The same rules are applied monthly to the production input data of the LGD engine, so that data quality in production can be compared with data quality at development. The data used in the model are aggregated on a largely automated basis; the only manual step is the legacy product mapping described in section 4.1, which is documented, justified and controlled. Controls over risk data used in the LGD model follow the same standards as controls over accounting data, with data quality measured against the thresholds described above. The data quality dashboard for the LGD model is reported monthly to the model owner and quarterly to the Credit Risk Management Committee, i.e. more frequently than annually. Consistency is assessed between the RDS and the production input data, over the observation period, including the changes in the default definition described in section 3.2, and as logical consistency between related fields such as sale date and sale proceeds.

sections.heading: Completeness and timeliness
sections.text: Record-level completeness was confirmed by reconciling the set of default events with the default register and the set of recovery processes with RECOV; attribute-level completeness is 100% for 33 variables and above 96.9% for all others. Where data are incomplete, the gaps are identified and explained and their effect on the estimates is assessed: this concerns the indirect costs before 2012, the valuation date at origination before 2012 and the NHG claim details before 2011. Timeliness is measured as the lag between reference date and availability (five business days for AMS and HYPO, 20 business days for RECOV cost bookings) and as the currency of collateral values, which are indexed monthly. Aggregated LGD data are available within the reporting timelines for the monthly own funds calculation and within five business days for ad hoc analyses in stress situations. Validity and uniqueness rules confirmed that facility identifiers are unique per default event after removal of the 212 duplicates, and appropriateness of the data for the range of application is assessed in chapter 5. The data used in development and as model inputs are sufficiently precise to avoid material distortions of pool assignment and contain no identified biases that make them unfit for purpose.

sections.heading: Data deficiencies
sections.text: Identified data deficiencies are recorded in the data deficiency log of MDL-02, each with identifier, affected variables and segments, data quality dimension, cause, quantified impact and treatment, and each is linked to a margin of conservatism category. DD-LGDM-01: default flag approximated and probation not reconstructable for 2008–2015 (consistency); impact −0.2 percentage points on LRA; treatment MoC Category A1; limitations log L-03. DD-LGDM-02: indirect costs not allocated for processes closed before 2012 (completeness); appropriate adjustment by deflated unit costs, residual uncertainty MoC A2; limitations log L-04. DD-LGDM-03: 94 legacy defaults without cash flows (completeness); exclusion and MoC A4; limitations log L-05. DD-LGDM-04: valuation date at origination missing for 3.1% of pre-2012 facilities (completeness); imputation, MoC assessed and rejected as the effect is below 0.01 percentage points. DD-LGDM-05: NHG claim details missing before 2011, claim payments recorded as a single recovery (accuracy); mapping by claim date, MoC assessed within A3. Every deficiency not fully remediated is assessed for inclusion in the MoC as Category A under CRM-STD-101, and the log references the MoC component to which it is mapped. Each deficiency has a remediation owner and target date or is documented as permanent (DD-LGDM-01, -02 and -03), is closed only on confirmed remediation, and the related MoC component is reassessed at closure.

sections.heading: Expert judgement in data treatment
sections.text: Expert judgement applied in data treatment is recorded in the expert judgement log of MDL-02 (EJ-LGDM), which is stored with the model documentation and referenced here and in chapter 11 of the MDD. Two judgements concern data treatment: EJ-LGDM-01, the approximation rule of the default flag for 2008–2015, and EJ-LGDM-02, the mapping of legacy HYPO-L product codes, whose version-controlled input file is the only manual input to the RDS build. EJ-LGDM-01 addresses data deficiency DD-LGDM-01 and is linked to MoC component A1; its log entry records the rationale, the evidence (the 2016–2019 overlap analysis), the alternatives considered and rejected (a 60-days-past-due proxy and exclusion of 2008–2015), the quantified impact (−0.2 percentage points), proposer, approver and approval date, and review date and expiry condition. The rationale is specific enough for a third party to replicate its effect, as the approximation rule is implemented in module default_flag_legacy.py. EJ-LGDM-01 is classified as medium materiality and was approved by the model owner and the head of development after challenge by an independent senior modeller of the PD team; the proposer was not an approver. EJ-LGDM-02 is of low materiality; its impact cannot be quantified separately but affects only product labels, and it was nevertheless classified as medium in line with MRM-STD-023 section 4.4 for a Tier 1 model.

sections.heading: Personal data and fair treatment
sections.text: The RDS contains personal data of natural persons (obligors and co-obligors of mortgage loans), which are processed for the development, validation and application of the IRB model on the lawful basis of legal obligation (Article 6(1)(c) GDPR, in conjunction with CRR Articles 144 and 179), recorded in the Record of Processing before processing started. The purposes of development, validation and application are specified in the Record of Processing entry RoP-CR-0412, which is referenced in the model inventory record of MDL-02. The data were collected for the administration of mortgage loans; their reuse for credit risk modelling is supported by the compatibility assessment CA-2024-031 under Article 6(4) GDPR, which considers the link between purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the consequences for data subjects and the safeguards applied. Legitimate interests are not relied upon for this processing, so no legitimate interest assessment is required. The model inventory records that personal data are processed and references the DPIA DPIA-2024-077. A DPIA was performed before processing, as the model is Tier 1 and uses personal data for decisions on capital and pricing (DPIA-2024-077, approved 18 November 2024). The DPIA describes the processing and its purposes, assesses necessity and proportionality, assesses the risks to data subjects and sets out the measures to address them, including pseudonymisation, access restriction and retention limits. The Data Protection Officer's advice of 6 November 2024 is documented in the DPIA; the residual risk was assessed as low, so prior consultation of the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens was not required. The DPIA is reviewed on every material change, including new personal data attributes, and at least every three years; the next review is due in November 2027. Compliance with the processing principles is demonstrated by the DPIA, the Record of Processing, the access logs of the analytics environment and the retention evidence, which together allow the Bank as controller to demonstrate compliance.

sections.heading: Data minimisation, pseudonymisation, retention and fair treatment
sections.text: Personal data attributes in the RDS are limited to those relevant to the model purpose: loan and collateral characteristics, income at origination, employment type (self-employed flag), arrears history, household composition (number of obligors) and recovery data; names, addresses and dates of birth are not included, and each attribute is justified in Annex A. Development and validation use pseudonymised data: customer and facility identifiers are replaced by keyed tokens, with the keys held by the Data Custodian of Group Data Management, and re-identification requires a documented, Privacy Office-approved purpose and is logged. The RDS is held only in the approved secure analytics environment of Risk (RAE) with role-based access for the model developers and Model Validation, and it is protected against unauthorised processing and accidental loss. Test environments of the LGD engine use masked production data only. Personal data are accurate at extraction and are kept up to date through the monthly refresh; corrections in source systems are propagated in the next RDS version. No special categories of personal data are processed, and no personal data are transferred outside the EEA. Annex A lists for each personal data attribute its purpose in the model, the lawful basis, the pseudonymisation applied and the retention period. The frozen RDS and development snapshots are retained for the period of use of the model plus five years after decommissioning, after which personal data are deleted or irreversibly anonymised and the deletion is evidenced in the retention log. Protected attributes (nationality, gender, age, marital status and ethnicity) are excluded from the candidate risk drivers. Candidate drivers were screened for proxy effects: the province of the property is used only at the level of four province groups within the house price index and the LGL component, and household composition and the self-employed flag were tested for correlation with age and gender, with no correlation above 0.2. Age is not used in the model. The results of the proxy screening are documented in Annex B, table B.9, and the MDD documents the outcome testing of the final model.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS is built by versioned code in the repository rds-lgd-mort-nl of the Bank's GitLab, tag v3.1.0, from the source snapshots of 7 February 2025, in the environment Python 3.11.7 with pandas 2.1.4 and the locked dependency file requirements-lock.txt. All extraction, transformation, exclusion, default flag construction and variable derivation steps are performed by build code; no manual data manipulation is used. A full rebuild by a second developer on 24 February 2025 reproduced the frozen RDS exactly: 31,206 default events, 1,184,650 cash-flow records and a total discounted recovery amount identical to the cent. The frozen RDS LGDMORT_RDS_v2025.1 is stored read-only in RAE with this version identifier, which is referenced in this document and in the MDD, and it was signed off by the model owner on 24 February 2025 before estimation started. The RDS version is archived together with the build code, its lineage and metadata, is retained for the life of the model and at least ten years after decommissioning, and is protected against alteration; corrections are made only on a new version with the original retained. Historical default, loss, recovery and exposure data are retained since 2008, exceeding the observation periods required by CRR Articles 179 to 181. Every count, share and rate in this document is produced by the reporting notebook rds_report.ipynb from the frozen RDS version referenced above.

sections.heading: Data dictionary and lineage
sections.text: The data dictionary lists all 41 RDS variables with business definition, source system and field, transformation, lineage and data quality rules; the table below summarises the main groups. Each critical data element has a business definition, a technical definition and at least one data quality rule per applicable dimension, for example OUTST_DEF (outstanding amount at default: principal plus accrued interest and fees at the date of default; HYPO.LOAN_BAL + AMS.ARR_INT; rules on completeness, reconciliation to HYPO and non-negativity). Identifiers and dates (11 variables): FAC_ID, CUST_ID, DEF_CHAIN_ID, DEF_DATE, CURE_DATE, SALE_DATE, CLOSE_DATE, PROB_START and reference dates, sourced from HYPO and AMS. Target constituents (18 variables): outstanding amount at default, write-offs, recoveries by source, direct costs, indirect cost allocation, additional drawings, EURIBOR at default, discount factors and realised LGD at default and per reference date, sourced from RECOV, GL and market data. Candidate risk drivers (12 variables): indexed LTV, NHG flag and guarantee amount, lien rank, property type, province group, interest-only share, loan age, self-employed flag, arrears in the preceding 12 months, loan size and loan-to-income at origination, sourced from HYPO, CVD and AMS. Table A.3 maps every UTP trigger to its source-system field, and table A.4 lists the personal data attributes with purpose, lawful basis, pseudonymisation and retention.

sections.heading: Representativeness analyses
sections.text: Annex B contains the detailed tables supporting chapter 5: B.1 defaults, closure rates and realised LGD per default year; B.2 PSI per risk driver and per pool between the RDS and the portfolio at 31 December 2024; B.3 cure rates, LGL and time in default per default year and calibration segment; B.4 comparison of the three default definitions on 2016–2019; B.5 before-and-after comparisons for changes in lending standards and recovery policy; B.6 multiple default and re-default analysis; B.7 impact of exclusions; B.8 recovery patterns of closed and incomplete processes; B.9 proxy screening results. Table B.3 shows for each default year the number of defaults returning to non-defaulted status within a fixed horizon of 24 months, the cure rate falling from 76.0% for 2008 defaults to 64.8% for 2013 defaults and rising to 83.5% for 2019 defaults. Table B.3 also shows the time in default per default year, which increased from a mean of 13 months for 2008 defaults to 19 months for 2013 defaults and decreased to 8 months for 2021 defaults. Table B.8 shows annual recoveries by source (sale proceeds, NHG claims, obligor payments, savings set-off and settlements), irrespective of default date and with and without auction sales, with sale proceeds relative to indexed value declining by 11 percentage points between 2010 and 2013. For incomplete recovery processes, table B.8 shows marginal recoveries per year after default, whose patterns for each default year are compared with those of complete processes of the same default year. The analyses are reproduced by notebook annex_b.ipynb from the frozen RDS.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Annex C justifies the treatment of every variable with missing values or outliers and reports the share of affected records. Valuation date at origination: 3.1% missing for pre-2012 facilities (data deficiency DD-LGDM-04); imputed with the deed registration date from the Kadaster, which in 2012–2014, where both are available, lies on average 23 days after the valuation date; effect on indexed LTV below 0.3 percentage points. Property type: 1.4% missing at random; imputed with the mode per province group (single-family house); re-estimation of the LGL component with an 'unknown' category gives the same coefficients within their standard errors. Loan-to-income at origination: 11.8% missing for structural reasons (loans originated before income data were captured in 2006); the variable was not selected as risk driver, so no imputation is needed. Indexed LTV: capped at 250% for 37 facilities; no other outlier treatments apply, and no outliers in the target variable are capped or excluded. All treatments are implemented in the build code and applied identically by the production LGD engine, as confirmed in the implementation test report EVD-02-IMPL.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content, representativeness and data quality of the reference data set (RDS) of the LGD model for Dutch residential mortgages (LGD-MORT-NL, model identifier MDL-02, model version 3.1). The RDS serves the estimation and calibration of the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default used for the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach, and it is also the data basis for the annual review of estimates. The scope of application covers all retail exposures secured by residential property in the Netherlands booked in the Bank's mortgage administration system, including loans with a Nationale Hypotheek Garantie (NHG) and loans secured by second-ranking mortgage rights. The document follows the RDS template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A (v3.0); template sections that do not apply are retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification, and added sections are placed after the last template section of the relevant chapter. It replaces the data chapter of the legacy MDD v2.3 (2023), in line with the migration rule of MRM-STD-021 section 9.1. The RDS documentation is one of the four mandatory documents of MDL-02: the RDS documentation (this document), the MDD LGD Mortgages (EVD-02-MDD v1.0), the implementation specification IS-LGDM-3.1 with the implementation and testing report EVD-02-IMPL, and the monitoring plan in chapter 10 of the MDD. Figures in this document are produced from the frozen RDS LGDMORT_RDS_v2025.1, which is also referenced in chapter 3 of the MDD, so that the RDS documentation, the MDD and the implementation specification refer to the same data version. Documents referred to are identified with document identifier and version and are held in the controlled repository accessible to Model Validation, so that the documentation does not rely on undocumented knowledge. The applicable requirement set was derived from the requirement library at the start of the 2025 recalibration (requirement set RS-2025-022) and was used to plan the evidence in this document. In the 1LoD self-assessment, every evidence reference points to a section number of this approved version.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS contains all default events of in-scope facilities with a date of default between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2023 (16 years), with recovery cash flows, costs and status information observed up to the cut-off date of 31 December 2024. The unit of observation is the mortgage loan (facility), comprising all loan parts secured by the same mortgage deed; recovery cash flows are recorded monthly per facility. After the treatments described in chapter 4 the RDS holds 31,206 default events on 31,206 facilities of 28,470 unique obligors, and 1,184,650 facility-months of cash-flow records. Of the 31,206 default events, 29,418 (94.3%) relate to closed recovery processes and 1,788 (5.7%) to incomplete recovery processes, mainly defaults of 2021 to 2023. The observation period exceeds the minimum of five years required by CRR Article 181(2) for retail LGD and includes all relevant internal loss data available in the Bank's systems; it consists of consecutive years up to and including the most recent complete default year. All defaults observed in the observation period within the range of application are included, except the technical past due situations and duplicate records described in section 4.2 and the 94 legacy defaults without cash-flow history.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts in January 2008 because the workout database of Financial Restructuring & Recovery (FR&R) holds complete facility-level recovery cash flows from that date; recovery data before 2008 were kept at aggregated portfolio level only and cannot be allocated to facilities. The window covers the global financial crisis of 2008–2009, the Dutch housing market correction of 2008–2013 (nominal house prices fell by 21% peak to trough), the peak in mortgage arrears in 2013–2014, the benign years 2016–2021 and the interest rate increases of 2022–2023. It therefore contains a representative mix of good and bad years and includes the downturn period identified in chapter 5 of the MDD, so that the long-run average LGD is representative of long-run experience. The economic conditions in the window are considered relevant for current and foreseeable conditions: the legal framework for forced sales (Article 3:268 of the Dutch Civil Code), the NHG scheme and the Bank's recovery process have remained in place throughout, while the effects of changes are analysed in section 5.1.3. With 31,206 defaults and 6,382 closed liquidation cases the number of observations is sufficient for robust estimation of the cure and liquidation components in both calibration segments, the smallest pool containing 611 defaults. Defaults under the definition of default implemented on 1 December 2020 are included from that date; in each annual review the window is extended with the most recent default year so that the share of defaults under the current definition increases, and the related MoC is reassessed.

sections.heading: Default cohorts and status of recovery processes
sections.text: Annex B, table B.1 shows per default year the number of defaults, the share of closed recovery processes and the average realised LGD over all defaults of that year that are closed or have reached the maximum recovery period of 60 months. Default counts rise from 1,212 in 2008 to a peak of 3,634 in 2013, fall to 1,009 in 2021 and increase again to 1,529 in 2023. A recovery process is treated as closed when the facility has returned to non-defaulted status, has been fully repaid, has been written off after sale of the collateral and final settlement of the residual debt, or when the maximum recovery period of 60 months after default has been exceeded; closure is recorded without delay in the monthly RDS update. The maximum recovery period of 60 months is supported by the recovery pattern of closed processes: 98.6% of the discounted recoveries of closed liquidation cases are received within 60 months of default, and the marginal recovery after month 60 is below 0.2% of the outstanding amount at default. For the 1,788 incomplete recovery processes, the cash flows observed up to the cut-off date are retained in the RDS and future recoveries are estimated in the MDD on the basis of the observed recovery patterns of closed processes of comparable time in default, applying a conservative treatment where the pattern is uncertain. Annual default counts are reported at each reference date, so that as many points in time are available for the impact analysis as the data allow and no default years are merged.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: Not applicable in the sense of the template condition: the target is the realised LGD of the regulatory default event defined in section 3.3, and no fixed 12-month outcome horizon is used. Realised LGD is measured over the complete recovery process, from the date of default until closure or the maximum recovery period of 60 months, as specified in section 4.4. For the cure component the target is the binary outcome whether the facility returns to non-defaulted status within the recovery process; for the liquidation component the target is the loss given liquidation of facilities whose recovery process ended with the sale of the collateral or another non-cure closure. Both component targets are derived from the same default events, so that the same definition of default is applied to the historical observations used in the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and to the observations used by the mortgage PD model MDL-01 for the overlapping period 2012–2023. For defaulted exposures, additional targets are defined per reference date in default (section 4.4.4).

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: For default events between 1 January 2008 and 31 December 2015 the default flag is approximated, because the components of the current definition (daily days-past-due counters with materiality thresholds, UTP flags and probation status) have been captured in the source systems only since 1 January 2016 (CR-STD-110 section 9.3). For this period a default is set when the monthly arrears amount exceeds three monthly instalments and EUR 100 at a month-end, or when the arrears management system records a forced-sale procedure, a distressed restructuring or a bankruptcy or debt-rescheduling (WSNP) registration. On the 2016–2019 overlap period, the approximation identifies 96.8% of the defaults under the reconstructed current definition and generates 2.1% additional defaults; the resulting average realised LGD differs by -0.2 percentage points, the approximation producing slightly more cures. Probation periods cannot be reconstructed for 2008–2015; for these years a return to non-default is recognised only after three consecutive month-ends without arrears above the threshold, which is identified as data deficiency DD-LGDM-01 and covered by MoC component A1. From 1 January 2016 to 30 November 2020 the default flag is reconstructed from daily data with the current definition, and from 1 December 2020 the production default flag under CR-STD-110 v2.0 is used; each of the three definitions is analysed separately in Annex B, table B.4. The regulatory materiality threshold of EUR 100 and 1% has been applied in production since 1 December 2020, the date of application set by De Nederlandsche Bank, and the RDS field DEF_FLAG_SOURCE identifies for every default event whether the approximated, reconstructed or production flag applies.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: A default occurs when the obligor is more than 90 consecutive days past due on a material credit obligation or when the obligor is considered unlikely to pay, in accordance with CRR Article 178 and CR-STD-110. Days past due are counted from the first day on which both the absolute component of EUR 100 and the relative component of 1% of the materiality threshold for retail exposures are exceeded, and counting restarts at zero when either component is no longer exceeded. The absolute component is compared with the sum of all amounts past due owed by the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, and the relative component is that sum divided by the total on-balance-sheet exposure of the obligor to the Bank and its subsidiaries, excluding equity exposures. The relative threshold of 1% applied is the level set by De Nederlandsche Bank for all institutions in its jurisdiction; no lower internal threshold is used as a UTP indication. An obligor is defaulted under the past due criterion when both components are exceeded for 90 consecutive days, and the default flag is activated at the onset of the 91st consecutive day; no months-in-arrears proxy is used for the period covered by the production flag. Days past due are computed daily in the arrears management system (AMS), and the date of default is the first day on which any default criterion is met; it is recorded for every default event in the field DEF_DATE. Once the past due criterion is met the obligor is classified as defaulted without further expert judgement, unless a technical past due situation is confirmed. The thresholds are expressed in euro and all exposures in scope are denominated in euro, so that the currency provisions of Article 5 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 do not apply.

sections.heading: Level of application, joint obligations and contagion
sections.text: The definition of default is applied at obligor level, in line with the Bank's risk management practice for retail mortgages, where arrears management, forbearance and recovery decisions are taken per household; the level of application has not changed over the observation period. As the facility-level option for retail exposures is not used, the facility-level materiality threshold and the facility-level calculation of Article 1(3) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/171 do not apply. When an obligor defaults, all credit obligations of the obligor with the Bank, including consumer loans and current account overdrafts, are flagged as defaulted in all relevant systems. Most mortgages are joint credit obligations of two partners; a joint obligation is treated as a separate obligor in the materiality threshold calculation, and the default of the joint obligation is propagated to the individual exposures of both partners unless Credit Risk Management documents that the para 97 exceptions of EBA/GL/2016/07 apply. Contagion between connected obligors is assessed case by case by FR&R for obligors who also hold business loans; the outcome is recorded in the default register. The same definition of default is applied by all Group entities holding Dutch residential mortgages, so that the RDS does not combine different default definitions.

sections.heading: Counting of days past due
sections.text: Any amount of principal, interest or fee not paid on the due date is recognised as past due, including arrears on loan parts with deferred interest and on linked bank savings accounts. Where the payment schedule has been modified, days past due are counted on the basis of the modified schedule, and every modification granted because of financial difficulties is assessed as a potential distressed restructuring (section 3.4). Instalments suspended under the statutory or contractual payment holidays of 2020 are not counted as past due; the reasons for the suspensions were analysed and 214 obligors were assessed as unlikely to pay. Counting is suspended for disputed amounts only where the dispute is before a court or before the Dutch Financial Services Complaints Institute (Kifid). Technical past due is recognised only for data or system errors of the Bank, failures of the payment system and payment allocation time lags; each case is documented, corrected within 30 days and reviewed quarterly by Credit Risk Management, and wrong credit decisions are never treated as technical past due. The Bank's policy on the re-ageing of facilities, extensions and deferrals, renewals and the netting of accounts is documented in the arrears management procedure AMS-PRC-04 v3.2, which prohibits re-ageing without a formal forbearance decision. Technical past due events identified in the RDS (1,014 events) are removed from the set of defaulted exposures used for estimation (section 4.2).

sections.heading: Return to non-defaulted status, probation and multiple defaults
sections.text: An obligor returns to non-defaulted status only when no default trigger continues to apply, after a probation period of at least three months in which no past due or UTP condition is met, and after an assessment by FR&R that the improvement in credit quality is factual and permanent, including a review of payment behaviour and income. For obligors defaulted because of a distressed restructuring the probation period is at least 12 months from the latest of the restructuring, the default classification and the end of any grace period. During this period the obligor must make regular payments totalling at least the amount previously past due or written off, have no amount past due and show no UTP indication or doubt about full repayment, including for schedules with a large final instalment. The probation start date and probation status are recorded for every default event in the fields PROB_START and PROB_STATUS. A new triggering of a default event after return to non-defaulted status is treated as a new default, subject to the multiple default treatment in section 3.3.4. Where a facility defaults again within 12 months of returning to non-defaulted status, both events are treated as a single default starting on the first date of default; the 12-month period is longer than the nine months of EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 101 and is justified by the re-default analysis in Annex B, table B.6, which shows that 71% of re-defaults of mortgages occur within 12 months after cure. The RDS links default events of the same facility through the field DEF_CHAIN_ID; in the observation period 2,386 default events were merged into a preceding default, and the merged events are listed in Annex B, table B.6. For merged defaults the outstanding amount at the first default date is used and all cash flows of both events are included in the economic loss; the artificial cure cash flow of the first event is removed. The treatment is identical in the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and it is applied consistently in the annual review datasets.
