sections.heading: Final pool parameters
sections.text: Table 5.8 lists per pool the number of RDS defaults, the LRA LGD, the downturn LGD, the MoC and the final LGD before floor: LP01 2.9%, LP02 6.4%, LP03 8.7%, LP04 10.8%, LP05 14.9% (NHG) and LP06 3.1%, LP07 5.8%, LP08 9.7%, LP09 15.2%, LP10 21.4%, LP11 27.9%, LP12 35.6% (non-NHG). The pool LGDs increase monotonically with the pool number within each segment and are consistent with the LRA calibration per pool, so that the estimates are accurate and consistent quantitative estimates of risk. Where data are less informative, estimates are more conservative: the Category C MoC, derived from a bootstrap that resamples obligors, is larger for the segment with more dispersed realised LGDs (0.28 against 0.12 percentage points), and the MoC for incomplete recovery processes applies the 25th percentile recovery pattern. The parameter table is version controlled as PT-LGDM-3.1 and loaded into RCE through the change management process. Estimates were reviewed with the most recent data in the annual review of 2025 and will be reviewed at least annually and when new information comes to light.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: The final LGD consists of the best estimate, including appropriate adjustments, plus a margin of conservatism quantified under CRM-STD-101 and EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraphs 36–52, distinguishing Category A (data and methodological deficiencies), Category B (relevant changes) and Category C (general estimation error). Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 during the development of version 3.1 and are listed in table 6.1, including the triggers considered and rejected (for example missing limit history, which is not relevant for mortgages). For each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first, and the MoC covers only the remaining uncertainty; the MoC is not used to compensate for deficiencies that can be corrected through an adjustment. Each deficiency is linked to exactly one category and recorded in the MoC register of MDL-02 with a unique identifier, the affected parameters and segments and a reference to the data deficiency log. Deficiencies identified by validation, monitoring, Internal Audit or the supervisor are assessed for their effect on the estimates and added to the register within three months. The Bank thus applies a framework that identifies deficiencies in data and methods, applies appropriate adjustments and quantifies a margin of conservatism commensurate with the expected range of estimation errors.

sections.heading: Category A and B deficiencies
sections.text: A1, default flag approximation 2008–2015 (DD-LGDM-01): quantified by re-estimating the LRA with the alternative approximation that sets default at 60 days past due at a month-end, the most adverse plausible treatment; effect +0.30 percentage points in both segments. A2, indirect costs before 2012 (DD-LGDM-02): range between the deflated 2012 unit costs and unit costs increased by 50%; MoC +0.15 percentage points. A3, estimation of future recoveries for incomplete processes: range between the median and the 10th percentile recovery pattern; MoC +0.30 percentage points. A4, exclusion of 94 legacy defaults (DD-LGDM-03): +0.05 percentage points, rounding up the estimated effect of +0.03. B1, early-intervention programme since 2019: range of cure-rate effects between 2.0 and 6.0 percentage points; MoC +0.20 percentage points; B2, NHG 10% own-risk share since 2014 (NHG segment only): +0.15 percentage points from a scenario with the own risk applied to all historical NHG claims. Each deficiency is quantified individually per calibration segment before aggregation within its category, each MoC is non-negative and not lower than the adverse effect of the sensitivity analysis, and the deficiency with a favourable effect (the approximation of the default flag lowers the LRA) does not reduce other MoC components. All Category A and B MoC components are quantified by sensitivity or scenario analysis; expert judgement was not needed for the quantification.

sections.heading: Category C and aggregation
sections.text: Category C MoC for the general estimation error is quantified per calibration segment as the difference between the 90th percentile of the bootstrapped distribution of the LRA LGD (5,000 replications, resampling obligors, seed 20250301) and the LRA: 0.12 percentage points for NHG and 0.28 percentage points for non-NHG; it is strictly positive and reflects the dispersion of the estimator. The total MoC per calibration segment is the simple sum of the Category A, B and C MoCs without diversification: 1.27 percentage points for NHG and 1.28 percentage points for non-NHG. The final MoC is added to the downturn LGD best estimate of each pool, so that it covers the uncertainty of both the long-run average and the downturn calibration. MoC is quantified in absolute percentage points consistently within the rating system. The total MoC is below the 5 percentage point threshold of CRM-STD-101 section 7.2 for LGD, so no redevelopment assessment by the Model Risk Committee is required. The effect of the MoC on RWEA is EUR 402 million (Category A EUR 252 million, B EUR 86 million, C EUR 64 million) and is reported per category in the quarterly MoC report.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power is measured with the generalised AUC (gAUC) of the pool assignment against realised LGD, as specified in the ECB validation reporting instructions, and with the AUC of the P(cure) component and the Spearman correlation of the LGL component. The gAUC is 0.702 on the development sample, 0.699 on the out-of-sample sample and 0.688 on the out-of-time sample, a relative decrease of 2.0%, within the 10% amber threshold of MV-HB-003; the Spearman correlation of LGL is 0.47, 0.45 and 0.43 respectively. Performance was tested for the whole model and for both calibration segments (gAUC 0.671 for NHG and 0.694 for non-NHG on the out-of-time sample) and for each pool. The results demonstrate that the model differentiates risk adequately between pools and has good predictive power, with input variables that form a reasonable and effective basis for the estimates and no material biases. Out-of-time and out-of-sample tests are part of the statistical validation process documented in chapter 10, which is repeated annually on new defaults.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and back-testing
sections.text: On the out-of-time sample, the realised LGD of closed processes (4.4%) is below the best estimate LGD of 5.9%; per pool, the one-sided paired t-test of realised versus estimated LGD does not reject the null hypothesis of no underestimation for any pool at the 5% level. Back-testing is performed at component level (realised versus predicted cure rates and LGL) and at facility level, because the model combines components. The back-testing uses all available defaults from 2008 onwards and is repeated annually in the review of estimates, with methods and data documented in the monitoring plan. The ELBE is back-tested against realised LGD at the reference dates in default with a two-sided paired t-test at portfolio and pool level; on 2021–2023 defaults the difference is not significant (p = 0.31). Methods and data used for back-testing are consistent with those of the previous model version; the change from the facility-level to the pool-level test in 2023 was documented, with both results reported in parallel in 2023.

sections.heading: Homogeneity and stability
sections.text: Homogeneity within pools and heterogeneity between adjacent pools were tested with the Kruskal–Wallis and pairwise Mann–Whitney tests on realised LGD at the 5% significance level; the initially six NHG pools were reduced to five, because the two lowest pools were not statistically distinct (EJ-LGDM-04). After the merge all adjacent pools are statistically distinct, and the coefficient of variation of realised LGD within pools is lower than across the segment, showing that pools group sufficiently homogeneous exposures and allow accurate estimation of loss characteristics at pool level. Stability over time was assessed with the pool distribution of the portfolio at year-ends 2016–2024 (PSI between consecutive years below 0.10) and with the coefficients re-estimated on 2008–2015 and 2016–2023 defaults, whose signs and magnitudes are consistent within two standard errors. The model therefore provides a meaningful differentiation of risk and consistent quantitative estimates.

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: The model was compared with the challenger direct beta regression (alternative A), which ranks risk less well (gAUC 0.684 against 0.702) and produces the same LRA by construction; no metric of the challenger is better than that of the model. The model was also compared with the previous version 3.0: the average final LGD decreased from 9.9% to 9.6% because of the inclusion of the 2021–2023 defaults with high cure rates. In the 2025 supervisory benchmarking exercise under CRD Article 78 (reference date 31 December 2024), the Bank submitted the LGD results for the residential mortgage benchmark portfolios in the prescribed templates together with an explanation of the methodology; the Bank's average LGD of 9.9% compares with a median of 12.4% for the EU sample and 10.1% for Dutch institutions. The ECB did not identify a significant divergence; the difference to EU peers is explained by the NHG share and the low indexed LTVs of the Dutch portfolio. External loss data of Dutch mortgages published by WEW for NHG loans were used as a further comparison: the NHG loss rate implied by the model is consistent with the WEW loss statistics for 2012–2016.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses covered the key assumptions and input data: maximum recovery period of 48 and 72 months (−0.10 and +0.05 percentage points on the LRA), discount rate add-on of 4 and 6 percentage points (−0.31 and +0.32), calibration window 2012–2023 (+0.6), inclusion of excluded technical past due events (−0.05), the alternative default flag approximations (+0.30 and −1.9) and the DP-B lag of 6 or 18 months (−0.4 and +0.2 on the downturn LGD). The results are documented with their effect on the final LGD in table 7.5 and were used to quantify the MoC components A1, A2, A3 and B1. The impact of every material expert judgement was quantified by sensitivity analysis under reasonable alternative judgements, as listed in chapter 11. No performance metric is outside its threshold; the amber PSI of indexed LTV between RDS and portfolio was analysed for its cause, recorded in the limitations log as L-06 and addressed by quarterly monitoring of the pool distribution.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: Material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (1) recovery patterns of closed processes are representative for incomplete processes; (2) the relation between indexed LTV and LGL observed in 2008–2023 remains valid; (3) the NHG scheme continues on its current terms; (4) the provincial house price index is an adequate proxy for the value of individual properties; (5) the model is used for Dutch owner-occupied residential mortgages only. The model does not work effectively for property types not represented in the RDS, such as buy-to-let or mixed-use properties, for defaults at the contractual maturity of interest-only loans, and in a scenario of house price falls exceeding the 21% observed in the RDS. Assumptions (2) and (4) are monitored through the quarterly back-testing and the annual review of estimates. Approximations used in risk reports based on the model output, such as the indexed LTV based on provincial indices, are documented here and their reliability is supported by the back-testing results.

sections.heading: Limitations log
sections.text: The limitations log of MDL-02 is contained in this section; each entry states an identifier, description, source, estimated impact, mitigating measure and owner. L-01 incomplete recovery processes (5.7% of defaults; impact covered by MoC A3; owner model developer); L-02 indexation with provincial rather than local indices (impact not significant in back-testing; monitored); L-03 default flag approximation 2008–2015 (MoC A1); L-04 indirect costs before 2012 (MoC A2); L-05 exclusion of legacy defaults (MoC A4). L-06 shift of the indexed LTV distribution relative to the RDS (monitored quarterly); L-07 no observations of defaults at contractual maturity of interest-only loans (monitoring of maturities from 2030; owner Retail Credit Risk Management); L-08 NHG own-risk share observed on few defaults (MoC B2). The log is kept up to date at each monitoring cycle and annual review; material limitations were reported to the approval authority at gate G3 and are recorded in the model inventory. Known limitations are communicated to model users in the annual user note.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: The model is implemented in the Bank's regulatory capital engine (RCE) according to the implementation specification IS-LGDM-3.1 v1.0, approved by the model owner on 14 April 2025 and consistent with this MDD; the implementation and its testing are documented in EVD-02-IMPL. The handover package to implementation contained the implementation specification, the final coefficients and parameter table PT-LGDM-3.1, 1,240 test cases and the reference outputs of the development code for the full RDS and for the portfolio at 31 March 2025. Implementation testing, the reconciliation of production and development outputs on identical input data, the parallel run and user acceptance testing were completed before version 3.1 was used in production on 30 June 2025. The system used for the calculation of own funds requirements applies the IRB risk weight formula for retail exposures secured by residential property with the model LGD, and its correct implementation was tested as part of the implementation of version 3.1. The production code, the implementation specification and this MDD are consistent, and the model owner confirms their consistency after each change and at least annually, most recently on 16 March 2026.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: The monitoring plan of MDL-02, approved by the model owner before the go-live of version 3.1 and reviewed by Model Validation, defines the KPIs, their calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, reference periods, segments, responsible persons and escalation per traffic light. KPIs: (K1) back-testing of realised versus estimated LGD on closed processes, one-sided t-test with amber at p < 5% and red at p < 1%, and portfolio underestimation above 5% relative amber and above 10% red; (K2) gAUC relative decrease versus development above 10% amber and above 20% red; (K3) PSI of the pool distribution and of each risk driver, amber from 0.10 and red from 0.25; (K4) realised versus predicted cure rate; (K5) ELBE back-test; (K6) production data quality; (K7) override rate; (K8) model coverage; (K9) share of EAD with binding floor. KPIs are computed for the whole model, for both calibration segments and for each pool. Monitoring is performed quarterly, as required for Tier 1 models, and results are finalised within 60 calendar days after the reference date. The monitoring plan is updated with each model change and reviewed at least annually.

sections.heading: Escalation and review of estimates
sections.text: Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive quarters, is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, with a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or a restriction of use, with changes processed under MRM-STD-050; red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the Model Risk Committee. Monitoring results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and for an additional MoC. The framework for the review of estimates defines the minimum scope and frequency of analyses, the metrics, thresholds and significance levels above, and the predefined actions for adverse results, and it reviews the estimates whenever new information comes to light and at least annually. A deviation of realised from estimated LGD beyond the red threshold, taking the position in the economic cycle into account, calls the estimates into question and leads to an upward revision where realised values continue to exceed expectations; a red outcome or an annual review concluding that estimates are inadequate leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months.

sections.heading: Annual review
sections.text: The annual model review covers the monitoring results, portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and the consistency between code and documentation; it concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose and is signed off by the model owner and submitted to MRM. It analyses the representativeness of the RDS for the application portfolio, model performance and its stability on the whole application portfolio without development exclusions, and whether recent data materially change the long-run average LGD, with back-testing per pool. It compares realised LGD with estimates and is provided to Model Validation. The regular cycle of validation includes the monitoring of performance and stability, the review of the model specification and the testing of outputs against outcomes. Monitoring code and data are version controlled in the repository lgd-mort-monitoring and monitoring results are reproducible.

sections.heading: Expert judgement
sections.text: Every expert judgement applied in the development is recorded in the expert judgement log EJ-LGDM of MDL-02, referenced here, and has been documented and approved before the model was used. EJ-LGDM-01 default flag approximation 2008–2015 (medium; −0.2 percentage points on LRA); EJ-LGDM-02 legacy product mapping (medium); EJ-LGDM-03 maximum recovery period of 60 months (low; −0.04); EJ-LGDM-04 merge of the two lowest NHG pools (low; +0.01 on LP01); EJ-LGDM-05 lag of 12 months for the DP-B impact window (medium; +0.4 on the downturn LGD relative to a 6-month lag). Each entry records the rationale, evidence and rejected alternatives, the proposer, approver and approval date, and a review date with expiry conditions; the design judgements EJ-LGDM-03 to -05 are justified in sections 4.6, 7.3 and 5.3 of this MDD. Medium judgements were challenged by an independent senior modeller and approved by the model owner and the head of development; the aggregate effect of all expert judgements is +0.17 percentage points on the final LGD (1.8% relative), below the high materiality threshold, so MRC approval of the aggregate is not required. The impact of human judgement on model performance was analysed: without the judgements the out-of-time gAUC changes by less than 0.002, and every judgement is justified by the evidence referenced in its log entry. Human judgement is used to a limited extent, as the number of relevant observations is large; no higher MoC for extensive judgement is required. Each judgement is reviewed at the annual model review and when new data could replace it; EJ-LGDM-06 (a 2021 add-on for payment holidays) was withdrawn in 2024 and is recorded as withdrawn in the log.

sections.heading: Overrides and overlays
sections.text: Pool assignment of performing exposures cannot be overridden; for defaulted exposures, FR&R may override the collateral value used for the ELBE only for three admissible reasons in a closed list (signed sale agreement, new full valuation not yet loaded, confirmed fraud), based on information not captured by the model. The override policy limits the change to the documented evidence value and requires approval by an FR&R senior credit officer independent of the case handler; positive overrides that lower the ELBE by more than 5 percentage points additionally require approval by Retail Credit Risk Management, making the policy more restrictive for favourable overrides. Every override is recorded in RECOV with reason code, written rationale, supporting evidence, proposer and approver. Override rates, direction and magnitude are monitored quarterly by reason and approving unit (2.1% of defaulted facilities in 2025, below the 5% retail threshold), and the performance of overridden cases is analysed annually by comparing realised LGD with the ELBE before and after override, including the performance of the approving officers. No overlays or post-model adjustments are applied to version 3.1; the model is complemented by human oversight through the review of FR&R case managers and the quarterly monitoring, which detect errors from model weaknesses using information not considered by the model.

sections.heading: Approvals and references

sections.heading: Version and change history of the rating system
sections.text: The register of rating system versions in the model inventory records all current and historical versions with approvals, changes and dates: v1.0 (IRB permission December 2007), v2.0 (2016 redevelopment, permission 2017), v3.0 (2021 redevelopment for EBA/GL/2016/07, EBA/GL/2017/16 and EBA/GL/2019/03), v3.0.1 (2023, correction of the indirect cost allocation) and v3.1 (2025 recalibration). Version 3.0 was a material change requiring prior permission (Class A): it was validated before submission, approved by the Model Risk Committee on 15 June 2021 (decision MRC-2021-033, quorum including the Head of Model Validation), and material aspects of the rating process were approved by the Management Board on 29 June 2021 on the MRC recommendation. The application was submitted to the ECB on 30 July 2021, after internal approval; version 3.0 was used for own funds requirements only after the ECB permission of 2 November 2022 and was implemented on 31 January 2023, within three months of the notification of the permission. Version 3.1 was classified by the developer as internally non-material and regulatory Class C (RWEA impact −2.1% in the range of application and −0.3% at Bank level at 31 December 2024; no qualitative criterion met; the extension of the time series consists only of the inclusion of the most recent observations), and the classification was approved by MRM on 11 March 2025. Version 3.1 was approved by the model owner on 30 May 2025 after MRM's confirmation of the classification, recorded as a new version in the inventory, and notified to the ECB in the quarterly ex post notification of 15 October 2025.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: This model development document (MDD) describes the design, methodology, calibration, performance and limitations of the LGD model for Dutch residential mortgages (LGD-MORT-NL, model identifier MDL-02, model version 3.1), in accordance with the MDD template of MRM-STD-021 Annex B, whose chapter structure, numbering and headings it follows. The model produces, for every mortgage facility in the range of application, the downturn LGD for performing exposures and the ELBE and LGD in-default for defaulted exposures, used for the calculation of own funds requirements under the A-IRB approach. It is documented in sufficient detail for Model Validation to understand the model, to reproduce its estimation and calibration from the frozen RDS and tagged code, and to assess its limitations without recourse to the developers. Cover block: document version 1.0, status Approved, author S. de Vries, reviewer T. Jansen, approvers E. van Dijk (model owner) and R. Kuipers (Head of Credit Risk Modelling), approval date 24 April 2026. The model is managed under the Model Risk Management Policy MRM-POL-001 as an internally developed quantitative method whose output is used for risk measurement, capital and pricing decisions, and it is registered in the model inventory since 2005 under MDL-02.

sections.heading: Range of application and exposure class assignment
sections.text: The range of application comprises all retail exposures to natural persons secured by residential property located in the Netherlands and booked by the Bank, including NHG-guaranteed loans, loans with second-ranking mortgage rights and loans in arrears; at 31 December 2025 it contains 368,512 facilities of 341,870 obligors with an EAD of EUR 61.8 billion. Exposures are assigned to the retail exposure class, sub-class secured by residential property, by the documented exposure class assignment module of the credit risk data warehouse, which applies the assignment sequence of the Bank's exposure class policy consistently over time. The retail criteria are met because the exposures are to natural persons, are part of a large pool managed on a pooled basis, and are monitored monthly against the retail thresholds. Own LGD estimates are used only for these retail exposures; no exposures to institutions, financial sector entities or large corporates are in scope, which are treated under the Foundation IRB approach where applicable. The IRB approach applies to all exposures of the retail real estate exposure class: the roll-out plan agreed with De Nederlandsche Bank in 2007 was completed in 2012 with the inclusion of the former brand portfolio, the plan was not used selectively to lower own funds requirements, and no sequential implementation is pending for this class. Mortgages on property outside the Netherlands (EUR 38 million, 0.06% of the class) are under permanent partial use of the Standardised Approach with the permission of the competent authority, being immaterial in size and perceived risk profile; the conditions are monitored quarterly with triggers on number of obligors (500), EAD share (0.5%) and average risk weight, and have remained fulfilled.

sections.heading: Intended use, users and use test
sections.text: Intended uses are the calculation of own funds requirements (regulatory use A-IRB LGD); secondary uses are risk-adjusted pricing of new mortgages, the credit risk appetite metrics for Retail (expected loss and RWA density), the internal capital allocation in the ICAAP, the IFRS 9 ECL model MDL-07 and management reporting. Main users are Regulatory Reporting, Retail Mortgages Pricing, Retail Credit Risk Management, Capital Management and IFRS 9 Modelling. The LGD estimates play an essential role in the risk management and decision-making process: they determine the risk premium in the pricing of every new mortgage, the approval authority for loans with an indexed LTV above 90%, the limits on high-LTV production in the risk appetite, and the monitoring of the portfolio in the quarterly Retail Risk Report to the Management Board. The IRB LGD is used in the internal capital allocation process to allocate credit risk capital to the Retail business line. The risk parameters used in the credit risk appetite metrics are produced by this model, which is registered in the model inventory and approved under MRM-POL-001, and the appetite includes expected loss, RWA density and the non-performing exposure ratio of the mortgage portfolio with limits and early-warning triggers. LGD estimates have been used internally for risk measurement and management since 2005, more than three years before the IRB permission of 2008. The model is used only within its approved scope of application, and it was validated before first use and after each material change.

sections.heading: Differences between regulatory and internal parameters
sections.text: For IFRS 9, MDL-07 uses the best estimate LGD components without downturn adjustment, MoC and regulatory floor, conditioned on forward-looking house price scenarios; the removal of the MoC is documented in the MDD of MDL-07 and reconciled annually with this model. The pricing tool and the risk appetite use the final IRB LGD per pool including downturn, MoC and floor, so that no difference to the own funds parameter exists for these uses. The use of different estimates for IFRS 9 is reasonable because IFRS 9 requires unbiased, point-in-time estimates, whereas own funds require downturn-consistent and conservative estimates. Model limitations, conditions of approval and compensating controls relevant to users are communicated to Retail Mortgages Pricing and Retail Credit Risk Management through the annual user note LGD-MORT-UN-2025 and in the limitations log in chapter 8. The LGD model does not score or decide on individual natural persons: pricing uses the pool LGD as one input to a rate grid, and credit decisions remain with the acceptance process, so no automated individual decision within the meaning of Article 22 GDPR is taken on the basis of the model.

The model owner updates the record within ten business days of any change to a mandatory attribute and at each gate, and attests its completeness and accuracy quarterly; all mandatory attributes are complete. sections.heading: Model classification and AI Act assessment
sections.text: The inventory records, since gate G1 of version 3.0, that the model is not an AI system under Article 3(1) of the AI Act: it is a statistical model with fixed logic (logistic and fractional logit regressions and look-up tables), it does not infer outputs autonomously beyond the rules defined by the developers, and it does not adapt after deployment. The complexity assessment of 12 January 2026 classifies the model as of medium complexity; it is not labelled highly complex or dynamic, as it uses no machine-learning techniques and is recalibrated only through the change process. The Bank's written model risk management policy MRM-POL-001 defines what constitutes a model, sets out the Bank's interpretation of model risk and describes the components of the model risk framework, under which this model is managed. A model identification questionnaire was submitted for the model at its registration in 2005, and the model was re-registered with model identifier MDL-02 at the inventory migration of 2019; the registration and version history are held in the model inventory. The model owner has not changed since 2021; the handover note of the previous owner, listing open findings, conditions, limitations and dispensations, is stored in the inventory.

The Bank's written model risk management policy MRM-POL-001 defines what constitutes a model, sets out the Bank's interpretation of model risk and describes the components of the model risk framework, under which this model is managed.

A model identification questionnaire was submitted for the model at its registration in 2005, and the model was re-registered with model identifier MDL-02 at the inventory migration of 2019; the registration and version history are held in the model inventory.
The model owner has not changed since 2021; the handover note of the previous owner, listing open findings, conditions, limitations and dispensations, is stored in the inventory.

sections.heading: Model design
sections.text: The LGD for a performing facility is estimated as LGD = P(cure) x LGC + (1 − P(cure)) x LGL, where P(cure) is the probability that the facility returns to non-defaulted status, LGC is the loss given cure and LGL is the loss given liquidation, which includes all non-cure closures. P(cure) is estimated with a logistic regression and LGL with a fractional logit regression on realised LGL of closed non-cure processes; LGC is estimated as the default-weighted average per calibration segment (1.2% overall), because its variation between facilities is small. The component structure reflects the Dutch mortgage recovery process, in which a default ends either with a cure after arrears are settled or a restructuring completes probation, or with the sale of the property under the right of summary execution, possibly followed by an NHG claim and collection of the residual debt. The facility-level estimate is used for risk differentiation only; risk quantification is performed at the level of 12 LGD pools, whose LGD is calibrated to the default-weighted average realised LGD of the RDS defaults in the pool and adjusted for downturn and MoC. For defaulted exposures, the ELBE and LGD in-default are estimated per reference date in default with the same component structure (chapter 5.6). The design and operational details of the rating system, the rationale for the choice of rating criteria and the major changes in the risk rating process since 2016 are documented in this MDD, which evidences compliance with the IRB requirements.

sections.heading: Segmentation and pools
sections.text: Two calibration segments are defined: NHG-guaranteed facilities (27.4% of facilities, 21.8% of EAD) and non-NHG facilities, because the loss profiles differ significantly (LRA LGD 4.1% versus 9.6%); no further geographical or product segments are needed, as all exposures are Dutch residential mortgages of the same product type. Facilities are assigned to 12 LGD pools, five in the NHG segment (LP01–LP05) and seven in the non-NHG segment (LP06–LP12), by the facility-level LGD score with fixed pool boundaries listed in table 2.1. Pool assignment takes into account obligor characteristics (self-employed status and delinquency in the past 12 months) and transaction characteristics (NHG guarantee, indexed LTV, lien rank, property type, region and interest-only share), in line with CRR Article 170(4). The pool definitions are mechanical and apply identically across all distribution channels, regional teams and legal entities, so that facilities posing similar risk are assigned to the same pool. Each pool contains at least 611 defaults in the RDS and at least 9,800 facilities in the current portfolio, and no pool holds more than 21% of EAD, so that pools are sufficient for quantification and validation without excessive concentrations. The scorecard coefficients, pool boundaries and pool LGDs in tables 4.3, 4.4 and 5.8 allow third parties to understand and replicate the assignment of each facility.

sections.heading: Assignment process and dependencies
sections.text: Pool assignment is fully automated in the Bank's regulatory capital engine (RCE) and updated monthly for every facility with the current indexed LTV, arrears history and NHG guarantee amount, which exceeds the annual update required for retail exposures and ensures that all relevant and current information is taken into account. Where an input is missing, the most conservative value of the pool assignment applies (for example indexed LTV above 110% when no valuation is available), so that less information leads to a more conservative assignment. Every facility has a valid pool assignment produced by the approved model before a credit decision is taken on an additional loan or restructuring. The model depends on the PD model for Dutch mortgages (MDL-01) through the shared default definition and RDS default flag, on the house price indexation of the collateral valuation database, and it provides inputs to the IFRS 9 model MDL-07 and to the ICAAP stress test satellite model MDL-10. In the ICAAP and EU-wide stress tests, the stress test satellite model projects pool migration and LGL under severe but plausible house price and unemployment scenarios, and the resulting LGD and own funds effects are integrated into capital planning.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The model is estimated on the approved RDS documented in EVD-02-RDS v1.0, frozen as LGDMORT_RDS_v2025.1, which contains 31,206 default events with default dates between January 2008 and December 2023 and cash flows observed up to 31 December 2024. The same default events and the same definition of default underlie the performing LGD, the ELBE and the LGD in-default, and the default flag is shared with the PD model MDL-01 for overlapping periods. The development, out-of-sample and out-of-time samples were defined before estimation: defaults of 2008–2020 were split randomly (seed 20250301, stratified by default year and NHG status) into a development sample (21,985 defaults) and an out-of-sample test sample (5,496 defaults); defaults of 2021–2023 (3,725 defaults) form the out-of-time sample, which was not used for variable selection or parameter estimation. The final calibration of the pool LGDs uses all 31,206 defaults, as required for the long-run average. RDS data deficiencies DD-LGDM-01 to -05 are cross-referenced to the limitations log in chapter 8 and to the MoC components in chapter 6.

sections.heading: Methodological alternatives
sections.text: Three alternatives were assessed against the criteria of MRM-STD-020 section 6.1 (regulatory compliance, data requirements, discriminatory power, stability, interpretability and implementation effort): (A) a direct beta regression of realised LGD, (B) the two-component cure and liquidation model and (C) a survival model of monthly recovery rates. Alternative A had the lowest discriminatory power (gAUC 0.684 on the out-of-sample sample) because the bimodal distribution of realised LGD, with 75% of values close to zero, is poorly captured by a single distribution. Alternative C achieved a comparable gAUC (0.699) but requires assumptions on censoring and the aggregation of monthly hazards, is less transparent to users, and its implementation in RCE would require a new calculation module. Alternative B was selected because it reflects the recovery process, performs best (gAUC 0.702), allows the downturn impact to be quantified per component and is directly interpretable by FR&R and Retail Credit Risk Management. The selected design is conceptually sound and consistent with the economic rationale of mortgage losses, which are driven by the probability of a cure and, if the property is sold, by the shortfall of the net sale proceeds relative to the outstanding amount.

sections.heading: Variable selection
sections.text: The long list of 12 candidate risk drivers combined the statistical analysis of the RDS with the input of FR&R, Retail Credit Risk Management and the literature, and covers all material drivers of cure and liquidation losses identified in these sources. Each candidate was assessed for economic rationale, availability at the point of use in RCE and stability over time (PSI over 2008–2023 below 0.25 per year pair), and the expected sign of each driver was stated before estimation in the development plan. Univariate analysis (information value for P(cure), Spearman correlation for LGL) reduced the list to nine drivers; the multivariate selection used stepwise estimation with a significance level of 1%, correlations above 0.6 were resolved by retaining the driver with the stronger rationale (indexed LTV was retained over loan age, correlation 0.64), and the final drivers were confirmed by expert review. All final drivers have the expected sign and a plausible magnitude, as shown in tables 4.3 and 4.4, so that the estimates are plausible, intuitive and based on the material drivers of the risk parameter. The rationale for the selected rating criteria and the supporting analyses are documented in Annex 2 of this MDD.

sections.heading: Cure probability component
sections.text: P(cure) is estimated by logistic regression on the development sample with the outcome that the facility returns to non-defaulted status within 60 months; drivers are measured at the reference date twelve months before default and, for exposures in default, at the reference date in default. Table 4.3 gives the coefficients: intercept 2.214; indexed LTV (per 10 percentage points) −0.187; arrears in the preceding 12 months (yes) −0.612; interest-only share above 50% −0.244; self-employed borrower −0.391; all significant at the 0.1% level. Higher indexed LTV reduces the probability of cure, because a sale without residual debt is not available to the obligor and refinancing is harder; prior arrears and self-employment indicate less stable income. The AUC of the P(cure) component is 0.741 on the development sample, 0.736 on the out-of-sample sample and 0.718 on the out-of-time sample. The cure component is estimated on the cure outcomes observed in the RDS, including the artificial cash flow at cure described in section 4.4.2 of the RDS documentation.

sections.heading: Loss given liquidation component and collateral
sections.text: LGL is estimated by a fractional logit regression on realised LGL of 6,382 closed liquidations and 846 other non-cure closures; table 4.4 gives the coefficients: intercept −2.905; indexed LTV at default (per 10 percentage points) +0.298; NHG −1.106; apartment +0.172; second-ranking lien +0.415; province group West −0.121. The LGL is not based solely on the estimated market value of the property: it reflects the observed sale discount relative to indexed value (8.4% for private sales and 27.6% for auctions), the time to sale of 21 months on average, the costs of sale and the risk that the Bank cannot gain control of and sell the property expeditiously. Potential decreases in collateral value between default and sale are reflected through the downturn calibration in chapter 5, in which house prices fell by up to 8.4% in a year; the model is not adjusted for potential increases in collateral value, and indexation uses the index at the reference date only. The dependence between the obligor's risk and the value of the property, both driven by house prices and unemployment, is addressed conservatively by calibrating the downturn LGL on defaults in the 2012–2014 downturn period, in which low house prices coincided with high default rates. Only collateral meeting CRR Article 181(1)(f) is used as risk driver; the prior-ranking claim is deducted for second-ranking liens, and no liability of the obligor is recognised as collateral. Mortgage deeds and the right of summary execution are enforceable in the Netherlands, the only relevant jurisdiction, as confirmed by the written legal opinion of external counsel of 12 March 2024, which is independent of the credit decision process and confirms that the Bank can liquidate the property within a reasonable time frame, including on insolvency of the obligor.

sections.heading: Recognition of the NHG guarantee
sections.text: The NHG guarantee of Stichting Waarborgfonds Eigen Woningen (WEW), which is backed by the State of the Netherlands, is unfunded credit protection recognised through the modelling approach: the NHG flag is a risk driver of LGL and NHG claim payments are recoveries of the guaranteed facilities, while LGD is adjusted and PD is not. The criteria for recognising the guarantee address the guarantor's ability and willingness to pay (WEW paid 94.1% of claims by number and 92.6% by amount in 2008–2023, rejections resulting from non-compliance with NHG norms), the timing of payments (on average four months after the claim), the absence of correlation with the obligor, and the residual risk from the 10% own-risk share for loans originated since 2014 and the annuity-based decline of the guarantee. There is no currency mismatch, WEW is not in default, and the correlation between WEW and individual obligors is negligible, so the conservative considerations of EBA/GL/2020/05 paragraph 34 have no quantitative effect. The enforceability of the NHG terms 2024 was confirmed by a written legal opinion of independent counsel; a new opinion is obtained when the NHG terms change substantively, most recently for the terms of 1 January 2024. Rejected claims are recorded as recoveries without protection with their source and are monitored, so that the LGL of the NHG segment reflects the observed rejection rate. The final risk weight of NHG-guaranteed exposures is not lower than that of a comparable direct exposure to the guarantor, which is verified monthly in RCE.

sections.heading: Allocation of recoveries and incomplete workouts
sections.text: The allocation of recoveries follows the recovery process: sale proceeds are applied first, then set-off of pledged savings, then the NHG claim on the remaining shortfall and finally collection of the residual debt, so that no protection is recognised twice. For NHG facilities with the 10% own-risk share, guarantor cash flows and guarantee-related costs are allocated to the covered part and other cash flows and direct costs to the uncovered part, with indirect costs allocated per EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraph 113; the covered and uncovered parts are not assigned to a separate scope, because substitution of risk parameters is not used. Future recoveries of the 1,788 incomplete recovery processes are estimated from the observed recovery patterns of closed processes with the same time in default and recovery status, back-tested on processes closed in 2023–2024 (estimated 97.2% of realised recoveries), with the recovery rate of the 25th percentile used for processes in the liquidation phase to account for the risk of lower or later recoveries; the residual uncertainty is covered by MoC component A3. Incomplete processes are included in the LRA with these estimated recoveries, so that LGD is estimated from realised LGDs of all defaults in the RDS. The maximum recovery period of 60 months (EJ-LGDM-03) is documented in the RDS documentation and supported by the observed pace of recoveries, which is consistent with the mortgage recovery process.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.text: Calibration is performed per LGD pool: the long-run average LGD of each pool is the default-weighted arithmetic average of the realised LGDs of all RDS defaults assigned to the pool, including estimated future recoveries for incomplete processes; averages of yearly averages are not used. Realised LGDs reflecting a profit are set to zero for the calculation of the observed and long-run average LGD, while the unfloored values are used for the ranking of the LGL component. The LRA LGD is 8.5% overall, 4.1% for the NHG segment and 9.6% for the non-NHG segment; the calibration is tested at pool level and at segment level, and no pool shows realised LGD above the estimate at the 5% significance level. Estimates are based on the Bank's own loss and recovery experience only and are not derived from market prices of financial instruments. The calibration therefore rests on historical experience and empirical evidence and is not purely judgemental; the expert judgements used are listed in chapter 11. The estimates are representative of long-run experience, since the observation period contains the downturn of 2008–2014 and the benign years that followed.

sections.heading: Identification of the economic downturn
sections.text: The economic downturn for the type of exposures 'retail exposures secured by residential property' was identified in January 2025 in accordance with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930, separately from the other types of exposures of the Bank. The relevant indicator set comprises GDP and the unemployment rate, BKR mortgage arrears registrations as externally provided aggregate default rate, NHG loss payments by WEW as externally provided aggregate credit loss, the PBK house price index per province group, and the number of forced sales at auction as additional indicator of the housing market cycle. The house price index is included once for each of the four province groups; a common national index was not used, because the co-movement of the provincial indices is strong (correlation above 0.95) but the amplitude of the 2013 decline differed by up to 6 percentage points. GDP and house prices are analysed in 12-month growth rates, the unemployment rate in levels and the default and loss indicators in 12-month sums, reflecting how each indicator is commonly reported and its ability to reveal cyclicality. For each indicator the most severe 12-month value was determined over the 20 years ending December 2024, considering 12-month periods starting in any month, not only calendar years. The 20-year time-span was assessed as representative of the likely future range of variability, as it contains the 21% house price correction of 2008–2013; the 1978–1982 decline was reviewed but not added, because the structural conditions of that period (unrestricted mortgage interest deductibility, no NHG, no LTV limits) differ materially, and the assessment is documented in Annex 3.

sections.heading: Downturn periods
sections.text: The most severe 12-month values are: GDP growth −9.1% (12 months to June 2020), house prices −8.4% (12 months to May 2013), unemployment 7.5% average (12 months to February 2014), BKR mortgage arrears registrations (12 months to June 2014), NHG loss payments (12 months to December 2014) and forced sales (12 months to March 2014). House prices, unemployment, arrears registrations, NHG losses and forced sales are significantly correlated and reach their most severe values within 19 months of each other; their downturn periods are merged into a single downturn period DP-B from June 2012 to December 2014, which covers all related peaks and troughs. DP-B is extended to December 2014 because the 12-month values of NHG losses and forced sales remained within 10% of their most severe values throughout 2014, reflecting the prolonged severity of the same housing market condition. GDP forms a separate downturn period DP-A from July 2019 to June 2020, equal to the 12-month period to which its most severe value relates, as no other indicator reached its most severe value in that period. The downturn periods are based on historically observed conditions and not on stress test scenarios, and they reflect cyclical rather than structural developments; the identification is reviewed annually and when new information comes to light, most recently in January 2026 without change.

sections.heading: Downturn impact analysis
sections.text: The impact analysis for DP-B shows, per default year, realised LGD averaged over all closed defaults or defaults that reached the maximum recovery period, rising from 7.1% in 2010 to 13.0% in 2012 and 12.2% in 2013 and falling to 5.8% in 2016. Cure rates within a fixed horizon of 24 months fell from 76.0% (2008 defaults) to 64.8% (2013 defaults); the average time in default of liquidations rose from 17 to 26 months; and sale proceeds relative to indexed value declined by 11 percentage points, with auction sales most affected. Marginal recoveries of incomplete processes of 2021–2023 follow the patterns of complete processes of the same default years. The analysis uses annual data points for every default year from 2008 to 2023 without merging years. A lag of up to 12 months between the downturn period and the visible impact on loss data was identified, as defaults of the second half of 2014 and early 2015 still showed elevated LGL; defaults up to June 2015 are therefore attributed to DP-B. For DP-A, no impact on realised LGD, cure rates or time in default is observed for defaults between July 2019 and June 2021, reflecting the payment holidays and support measures and continued house price growth. As relevant loss data are available during, before and after both downturn periods, downturn LGD is calibrated on the observed impact under Section 5 of EBA/GL/2019/03.

sections.heading: Downturn LGD quantification
sections.text: Downturn LGD is calibrated for each downturn period and each calibration segment by recalibrating the components on the defaults attributed to the period: for DP-B, P(cure) is shifted by a segment-specific log-odds adjustment to the cure rate observed in the period and LGL is scaled to the average LGL observed in the period, starting with LGL as the component with the highest observed impact and adding the cure-rate impact. Because both components are recalibrated on the same default cohort, their dependency in the downturn is reflected when they are aggregated into downturn LGD. Cash flows received more than 60 months after default, which may reflect the recovery of the housing market after the downturn, are excluded from the downturn calibration. Applied to the current performing portfolio, the average downturn LGD including final MoC is 14.4% for DP-B and 9.8% for DP-A; DP-B is selected as the final relevant downturn period for both calibration segments, with a downturn LGD best estimate of 6.3% for NHG and 14.9% for non-NHG facilities. Downturn LGD is calibrated at pool level and aggregated to calibration segment level, i.e. at least at the level of the long-run average calibration; the final downturn LGD plus final MoC exceeds the LRA LGD plus final MoC in both segments, so that the more conservative downturn estimate is used. The downturn LGD is estimated in accordance with EBA/GL/2019/03 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/930, applying the requirements of Sections 4 and 6 to 9 of EBA/GL/2017/16, and is documented per calibration segment in table 5.4. As observed impact is available, neither the haircut or extrapolation approaches of Section 6 nor the fallback of the LRA plus 15 percentage points of Section 7 is applied.

sections.heading: Comparison with the reference value and cyclicality
sections.text: Using all available loss data, the two default years with the highest ratio of total economic loss to total outstanding amount at default are 2012 (14.6%) and 2013 (13.8%). The reference value, computed per calibration segment as the simple average of the average realised LGDs of these two years, is 5.8% for NHG, 14.4% for non-NHG and 12.6% overall. The final downturn LGD (6.3% and 14.9%) exceeds the reference value in both segments, so no material difference requires justification or a re-assessment of the downturn quantification. As indexed LTV is a cycle-sensitive risk driver, the current pool distribution was compared with the distribution the portfolio would have under DP-B house prices (indexation at the May 2013 level): 34% of EAD would move to higher pools. The downturn LGD is calibrated per pool on the realised downturn LGDs of the facilities in that pool, which limits cyclicality, and no further adjustment was deemed necessary.

sections.heading: ELBE and LGD in-default
sections.text: An ELBE and an LGD in-default are assigned to every defaulted exposure; they are estimated per reference date in default (0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 36 and 48 months and signed sale agreement) as the default-weighted average realised LGD at that reference date, calculated on the outstanding amount at the reference date with subsequent cash flows discounted to it. The ELBE is the best estimate of expected loss given current economic circumstances and exposure status: it contains no MoC and reflects current circumstances through the indexed LTV at the reference date, an economically sensitive driver, so no separate adjustment of the long-run average is required. The LGD in-default equals the ELBE plus an add-on for unexpected losses during the recovery period, consisting of the downturn component, inferred per reference date as the difference between the DP-B calibrated LGD and the ELBE, and the MoC. The same downturn period DP-B as for non-defaulted exposures is used, so that LGD in-default reflects at least downturn conditions where more conservative than the LRA for defaulted exposures. LGD in-default exceeds the ELBE for all exposures; where the specific credit risk adjustment of an exposure exceeds its ELBE, the LGD in-default is increased by the difference. At 31 December 2025 the defaulted portfolio (2,146 facilities, EAD EUR 612 million) has an average ELBE of 9.8% and an average LGD in-default of 13.9%; the add-on of 4.1 percentage points consists of 2.9 percentage points downturn component and 1.2 percentage points MoC, with no additional unexpected-loss component.

sections.heading: Regulatory floors
sections.text: The final LGD of each performing exposure is floored at 5%, the input floor of CRR Article 164(4) for retail exposures secured by residential property, irrespective of the level of collateral. The floor is applied at exposure level after the downturn adjustment and the MoC; at 31 December 2025 it is binding for 41.3% of facilities and 36.8% of EAD, mainly in pools LP01, LP02 and LP06. The other retail input floors of Article 164(4) do not apply, because all exposures in scope are secured by residential property. The order of adjustments, from best estimate to downturn adjustment, MoC and floor, is identical in development and in RCE. After the floor, the EAD-weighted average LGD of the performing portfolio is 9.6%.

sections.heading: Final pool parameters
sections.text: Table 5.8 lists per pool the number of RDS defaults, the LRA LGD, the downturn LGD, the MoC and the final LGD before floor: LP01 2.9%, LP02 6.4%, LP03 8.7%, LP04 10.8%, LP05 14.9% (NHG) and LP06 3.1%, LP07 5.8%, LP08 9.7%, LP09 15.2%, LP10 21.4%, LP11 27.9%, LP12 35.6% (non-NHG). The pool LGDs increase monotonically with the pool number within each segment and are consistent with the LRA calibration per pool, so that the estimates are accurate and consistent quantitative estimates of risk. Where data are less informative, estimates are more conservative: the Category C MoC, derived from a bootstrap that resamples obligors, is larger for the segment with more dispersed realised LGDs (0.28 against 0.12 percentage points), and the MoC for incomplete recovery processes applies the 25th percentile recovery pattern. The parameter table is version controlled as PT-LGDM-3.1 and loaded into RCE through the change management process. Estimates were reviewed with the most recent data in the annual review of 2025 and will be reviewed at least annually and when new information comes to light.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: The final LGD consists of the best estimate, including appropriate adjustments, plus a margin of conservatism quantified under CRM-STD-101 and EBA/GL/2017/16 paragraphs 36–52, distinguishing Category A (data and methodological deficiencies), Category B (relevant changes) and Category C (general estimation error). Deficiencies were identified systematically with the trigger list of CRM-STD-101 Annex 1 during the development of version 3.1 and are listed in table 6.1, including the triggers considered and rejected (for example missing limit history, which is not relevant for mortgages). For each deficiency an appropriate adjustment was considered first, and the MoC covers only the remaining uncertainty; the MoC is not used to compensate for deficiencies that can be corrected through an adjustment. Each deficiency is linked to exactly one category and recorded in the MoC register of MDL-02 with a unique identifier, the affected parameters and segments and a reference to the data deficiency log. Deficiencies identified by validation, monitoring, Internal Audit or the supervisor are assessed for their effect on the estimates and added to the register within three months. The Bank thus applies a framework that identifies deficiencies in data and methods, applies appropriate adjustments and quantifies a margin of conservatism commensurate with the expected range of estimation errors.

sections.heading: Category A and B deficiencies
sections.text: A1, default flag approximation 2008–2015 (DD-LGDM-01): quantified by re-estimating the LRA with the alternative approximation that sets default at 60 days past due at a month-end, the most adverse plausible treatment; effect +0.30 percentage points in both segments. A2, indirect costs before 2012 (DD-LGDM-02): range between the deflated 2012 unit costs and unit costs increased by 50%; MoC +0.15 percentage points. A3, estimation of future recoveries for incomplete processes: range between the median and the 10th percentile recovery pattern; MoC +0.30 percentage points. A4, exclusion of 94 legacy defaults (DD-LGDM-03): +0.05 percentage points, rounding up the estimated effect of +0.03. B1, early-intervention programme since 2019: range of cure-rate effects between 2.0 and 6.0 percentage points; MoC +0.20 percentage points; B2, NHG 10% own-risk share since 2014 (NHG segment only): +0.15 percentage points from a scenario with the own risk applied to all historical NHG claims. Each deficiency is quantified individually per calibration segment before aggregation within its category, each MoC is non-negative and not lower than the adverse effect of the sensitivity analysis, and the deficiency with a favourable effect (the approximation of the default flag lowers the LRA) does not reduce other MoC components. All Category A and B MoC components are quantified by sensitivity or scenario analysis; expert judgement was not needed for the quantification.

sections.heading: Category C and aggregation
sections.text: Category C MoC for the general estimation error is quantified per calibration segment as the difference between the 90th percentile of the bootstrapped distribution of the LRA LGD (5,000 replications, resampling obligors, seed 20250301) and the LRA: 0.12 percentage points for NHG and 0.28 percentage points for non-NHG; it is strictly positive and reflects the dispersion of the estimator. The total MoC per calibration segment is the simple sum of the Category A, B and C MoCs without diversification: 1.27 percentage points for NHG and 1.28 percentage points for non-NHG. The final MoC is added to the downturn LGD best estimate of each pool, so that it covers the uncertainty of both the long-run average and the downturn calibration. MoC is quantified in absolute percentage points consistently within the rating system. The total MoC is below the 5 percentage point threshold of CRM-STD-101 section 7.2 for LGD, so no redevelopment assessment by the Model Risk Committee is required. The effect of the MoC on RWEA is EUR 402 million (Category A EUR 252 million, B EUR 86 million, C EUR 64 million) and is reported per category in the quarterly MoC report.

sections.heading: MoC documentation, monitoring and remediation
sections.text: This chapter and the MoC register record the MoC applied, the complete list of identified deficiencies and affected components, their category, the quantification method and value per calibration segment, and the remediation status. A1, A2 and A4 concern historical data that cannot be recovered and are documented as permanent deficiencies reassessed at each annual review; A3 is reduced as recovery processes close and has a remediation plan with the model developer as owner and annual target dates; B1 and B2 are reassessed as post-change defaults accumulate. MoC levels are monitored in the quarterly monitoring report and reassessed in the annual review of estimates after inclusion of the most recent data, and internal reporting shows the MoC separately for Categories A, B and C. An MoC component is reduced or removed only after remediation of the underlying deficiency has been implemented and confirmed by Model Validation. Changes in the MoC are classified as model changes under MRM-STD-050 and Delegated Regulation (EU) No 529/2014.

sections.heading: Discriminatory power
sections.text: Discriminatory power is measured with the generalised AUC (gAUC) of the pool assignment against realised LGD, as specified in the ECB validation reporting instructions, and with the AUC of the P(cure) component and the Spearman correlation of the LGL component. The gAUC is 0.702 on the development sample, 0.699 on the out-of-sample sample and 0.688 on the out-of-time sample, a relative decrease of 2.0%, within the 10% amber threshold of MV-HB-003; the Spearman correlation of LGL is 0.47, 0.45 and 0.43 respectively. Performance was tested for the whole model and for both calibration segments (gAUC 0.671 for NHG and 0.694 for non-NHG on the out-of-time sample) and for each pool. The results demonstrate that the model differentiates risk adequately between pools and has good predictive power, with input variables that form a reasonable and effective basis for the estimates and no material biases. Out-of-time and out-of-sample tests are part of the statistical validation process documented in chapter 10, which is repeated annually on new defaults.

sections.heading: Calibration accuracy and back-testing
sections.text: On the out-of-time sample, the realised LGD of closed processes (4.4%) is below the best estimate LGD of 5.9%; per pool, the one-sided paired t-test of realised versus estimated LGD does not reject the null hypothesis of no underestimation for any pool at the 5% level. Back-testing is performed at component level (realised versus predicted cure rates and LGL) and at facility level, because the model combines components. The back-testing uses all available defaults from 2008 onwards and is repeated annually in the review of estimates, with methods and data documented in the monitoring plan. The ELBE is back-tested against realised LGD at the reference dates in default with a two-sided paired t-test at portfolio and pool level; on 2021–2023 defaults the difference is not significant (p = 0.31). Methods and data used for back-testing are consistent with those of the previous model version; the change from the facility-level to the pool-level test in 2023 was documented, with both results reported in parallel in 2023.

sections.heading: Homogeneity and stability
sections.text: Homogeneity within pools and heterogeneity between adjacent pools were tested with the Kruskal–Wallis and pairwise Mann–Whitney tests on realised LGD at the 5% significance level; the initially six NHG pools were reduced to five, because the two lowest pools were not statistically distinct (EJ-LGDM-04). After the merge all adjacent pools are statistically distinct, and the coefficient of variation of realised LGD within pools is lower than across the segment, showing that pools group sufficiently homogeneous exposures and allow accurate estimation of loss characteristics at pool level. Stability over time was assessed with the pool distribution of the portfolio at year-ends 2016–2024 (PSI between consecutive years below 0.10) and with the coefficients re-estimated on 2008–2015 and 2016–2023 defaults, whose signs and magnitudes are consistent within two standard errors. The model therefore provides a meaningful differentiation of risk and consistent quantitative estimates.

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: The model was compared with the challenger direct beta regression (alternative A), which ranks risk less well (gAUC 0.684 against 0.702) and produces the same LRA by construction; no metric of the challenger is better than that of the model. The model was also compared with the previous version 3.0: the average final LGD decreased from 9.9% to 9.6% because of the inclusion of the 2021–2023 defaults with high cure rates. In the 2025 supervisory benchmarking exercise under CRD Article 78 (reference date 31 December 2024), the Bank submitted the LGD results for the residential mortgage benchmark portfolios in the prescribed templates together with an explanation of the methodology; the Bank's average LGD of 9.9% compares with a median of 12.4% for the EU sample and 10.1% for Dutch institutions. The ECB did not identify a significant divergence; the difference to EU peers is explained by the NHG share and the low indexed LTVs of the Dutch portfolio. External loss data of Dutch mortgages published by WEW for NHG loans were used as a further comparison: the NHG loss rate implied by the model is consistent with the WEW loss statistics for 2012–2016.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses covered the key assumptions and input data: maximum recovery period of 48 and 72 months (−0.10 and +0.05 percentage points on the LRA), discount rate add-on of 4 and 6 percentage points (−0.31 and +0.32), calibration window 2012–2023 (+0.6), inclusion of excluded technical past due events (−0.05), the alternative default flag approximations (+0.30 and −1.9) and the DP-B lag of 6 or 18 months (−0.4 and +0.2 on the downturn LGD). The results are documented with their effect on the final LGD in table 7.5 and were used to quantify the MoC components A1, A2, A3 and B1. The impact of every material expert judgement was quantified by sensitivity analysis under reasonable alternative judgements, as listed in chapter 11. No performance metric is outside its threshold; the amber PSI of indexed LTV between RDS and portfolio was analysed for its cause, recorded in the limitations log as L-06 and addressed by quarterly monitoring of the pool distribution.

sections.heading: Analysis of individual defaults and climate risk drivers
sections.text: For the smallest pools (LP04, LP05 and LP12, between 611 and 890 defaults), a sample of 60 individual defaults was reviewed with FR&R to verify that the main loss drivers, such as sale discount, prior liens and NHG rejections, are reflected in the model; no model change was made in response to individual events. The materiality of climate-related and environmental risks was assessed: energy label (available for 78% of properties sold since 2015) shows a sale discount 2.1 percentage points higher for labels E to G, which is not significant after controlling for property age and region, and flood risk under the Climate Impact Atlas scenarios is not material for the portfolio. Climate drivers are therefore not included, and their materiality is reassessed in each annual review as more sales data with energy labels become available. The review of individual defaults also confirmed that the model is used in line with the recovery process of FR&R.

sections.heading: Assumptions and limitations
sections.text: Material assumptions were identified and assessed for plausibility: (1) recovery patterns of closed processes are representative for incomplete processes; (2) the relation between indexed LTV and LGL observed in 2008–2023 remains valid; (3) the NHG scheme continues on its current terms; (4) the provincial house price index is an adequate proxy for the value of individual properties; (5) the model is used for Dutch owner-occupied residential mortgages only. The model does not work effectively for property types not represented in the RDS, such as buy-to-let or mixed-use properties, for defaults at the contractual maturity of interest-only loans, and in a scenario of house price falls exceeding the 21% observed in the RDS. Assumptions (2) and (4) are monitored through the quarterly back-testing and the annual review of estimates. Approximations used in risk reports based on the model output, such as the indexed LTV based on provincial indices, are documented here and their reliability is supported by the back-testing results.

sections.heading: Limitations log
sections.text: The limitations log of MDL-02 is contained in this section; each entry states an identifier, description, source, estimated impact, mitigating measure and owner. L-01 incomplete recovery processes (5.7% of defaults; impact covered by MoC A3; owner model developer); L-02 indexation with provincial rather than local indices (impact not significant in back-testing; monitored); L-03 default flag approximation 2008–2015 (MoC A1); L-04 indirect costs before 2012 (MoC A2); L-05 exclusion of legacy defaults (MoC A4). L-06 shift of the indexed LTV distribution relative to the RDS (monitored quarterly); L-07 no observations of defaults at contractual maturity of interest-only loans (monitoring of maturities from 2030; owner Retail Credit Risk Management); L-08 NHG own-risk share observed on few defaults (MoC B2). The log is kept up to date at each monitoring cycle and annual review; material limitations were reported to the approval authority at gate G3 and are recorded in the model inventory. Known limitations are communicated to model users in the annual user note.

sections.heading: Implementation
sections.text: The model is implemented in the Bank's regulatory capital engine (RCE) according to the implementation specification IS-LGDM-3.1 v1.0, approved by the model owner on 14 April 2025 and consistent with this MDD; the implementation and its testing are documented in EVD-02-IMPL. The handover package to implementation contained the implementation specification, the final coefficients and parameter table PT-LGDM-3.1, 1,240 test cases and the reference outputs of the development code for the full RDS and for the portfolio at 31 March 2025. Implementation testing, the reconciliation of production and development outputs on identical input data, the parallel run and user acceptance testing were completed before version 3.1 was used in production on 30 June 2025. The system used for the calculation of own funds requirements applies the IRB risk weight formula for retail exposures secured by residential property with the model LGD, and its correct implementation was tested as part of the implementation of version 3.1. The production code, the implementation specification and this MDD are consistent, and the model owner confirms their consistency after each change and at least annually, most recently on 16 March 2026.

sections.heading: Monitoring
sections.text: The monitoring plan of MDL-02, approved by the model owner before the go-live of version 3.1 and reviewed by Model Validation, defines the KPIs, their calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, reference periods, segments, responsible persons and escalation per traffic light. KPIs: (K1) back-testing of realised versus estimated LGD on closed processes, one-sided t-test with amber at p < 5% and red at p < 1%, and portfolio underestimation above 5% relative amber and above 10% red; (K2) gAUC relative decrease versus development above 10% amber and above 20% red; (K3) PSI of the pool distribution and of each risk driver, amber from 0.10 and red from 0.25; (K4) realised versus predicted cure rate; (K5) ELBE back-test; (K6) production data quality; (K7) override rate; (K8) model coverage; (K9) share of EAD with binding floor. KPIs are computed for the whole model, for both calibration segments and for each pool. Monitoring is performed quarterly, as required for Tier 1 models, and results are finalised within 60 calendar days after the reference date. The monitoring plan is updated with each model change and reviewed at least annually.

sections.heading: Escalation and review of estimates
sections.text: Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the monitoring report; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive quarters, is notified to MRM and Model Validation within ten business days, with a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or a restriction of use, with changes processed under MRM-STD-050; red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the Model Risk Committee. Monitoring results indicating non-compliance with the CRR are assessed for notification to the ECB and for an additional MoC. The framework for the review of estimates defines the minimum scope and frequency of analyses, the metrics, thresholds and significance levels above, and the predefined actions for adverse results, and it reviews the estimates whenever new information comes to light and at least annually. A deviation of realised from estimated LGD beyond the red threshold, taking the position in the economic cycle into account, calls the estimates into question and leads to an upward revision where realised values continue to exceed expectations; a red outcome or an annual review concluding that estimates are inadequate leads to a recalibration or redevelopment plan approved by the Model Risk Committee within three months.

sections.heading: Annual review
sections.text: The annual model review covers the monitoring results, portfolio and environment changes, open findings and data deficiencies, the expert judgement log and overlays, and the consistency between code and documentation; it concludes whether the model remains fit for purpose and is signed off by the model owner and submitted to MRM. It analyses the representativeness of the RDS for the application portfolio, model performance and its stability on the whole application portfolio without development exclusions, and whether recent data materially change the long-run average LGD, with back-testing per pool. It compares realised LGD with estimates and is provided to Model Validation. The regular cycle of validation includes the monitoring of performance and stability, the review of the model specification and the testing of outputs against outcomes. Monitoring code and data are version controlled in the repository lgd-mort-monitoring and monitoring results are reproducible.

sections.heading: Expert judgement
sections.text: Every expert judgement applied in the development is recorded in the expert judgement log EJ-LGDM of MDL-02, referenced here, and has been documented and approved before the model was used. EJ-LGDM-01 default flag approximation 2008–2015 (medium; −0.2 percentage points on LRA); EJ-LGDM-02 legacy product mapping (medium); EJ-LGDM-03 maximum recovery period of 60 months (low; −0.04); EJ-LGDM-04 merge of the two lowest NHG pools (low; +0.01 on LP01); EJ-LGDM-05 lag of 12 months for the DP-B impact window (medium; +0.4 on the downturn LGD relative to a 6-month lag). Each entry records the rationale, evidence and rejected alternatives, the proposer, approver and approval date, and a review date with expiry conditions; the design judgements EJ-LGDM-03 to -05 are justified in sections 4.6, 7.3 and 5.3 of this MDD. Medium judgements were challenged by an independent senior modeller and approved by the model owner and the head of development; the aggregate effect of all expert judgements is +0.17 percentage points on the final LGD (1.8% relative), below the high materiality threshold, so MRC approval of the aggregate is not required. The impact of human judgement on model performance was analysed: without the judgements the out-of-time gAUC changes by less than 0.002, and every judgement is justified by the evidence referenced in its log entry. Human judgement is used to a limited extent, as the number of relevant observations is large; no higher MoC for extensive judgement is required. Each judgement is reviewed at the annual model review and when new data could replace it; EJ-LGDM-06 (a 2021 add-on for payment holidays) was withdrawn in 2024 and is recorded as withdrawn in the log.
